Montreal and the National Capital Region experienced their wettest springs in recorded history with over +400 mm of rainfall. Several communities declared States of Emergency including Gatineau, Montreal, and many smaller towns. The Canadian military deployed 4,000 personnel to help with the flood efforts. The event caused significant losses including over $116 million in insured damage, and 550 damaged roads. Two people were killed in floodwaters in the Sainte-Anne River (Gaspe region).
provinces: NB NL NS ON PE QC

comment: A winter storm significantly impacted central, south-central, eastern and north-eastern New Brunswick as well as the Acadian Peninsula. Regions that were hardest hit were the Counties of Kent, Northumberland and Gloucester. Ice accumulation on power lines and poles caused over 600 poles to collapse. NB Power reported 130,000 customers that were without power (which is roughly 286,000 residents); some homes were without power for 12 days. Nearly a third of New Brunswick residents were impacted. The communities of Saint Marie-Saint Raphael, Le Goulet, Lameque and Tracadie-Sheila declared States of Local Emergency. The Canadian Armed Forces were deployed to help with the storm efforts. It is suspected that the unsafe use of generators and heating devices led to 2 deaths and 45 related illnesses/injuries.

A 3-day winter storm dropped 60 cm of snow with wind gusts of 120 km/hr and zero visibility. The blizzard lasted 57 hours; the third longest in Canadian history. Some snow drifts measured 25-30 ft and others up to 9 ft along major roads. Building and roof damage was also reported. Emergency services, critical facilities and VIA Rail service all experienced significant disruptions.  Following the event, the Town of Churchill declared a State of Local Emergency.

Following a relatively cold and dry winter, the Southern Interior region of British Columbia experienced a wetter than average spring. A late snowfall and rain accumulation led to saturated soils, overland flow, and slope instability throughout areas of the south and central Okanagan as well as the Kootenay and Shuswap regions. The flooding led to 2,500 evacuations which were mostly from the Okanagan. Numerous States of Local Emergencies were declared. 15 First Nation communities were impacted where the flooding damaged homes and infrastructure. The flood response costs alone were estimated to be $73 million.

A fast-moving severe storm with ping pong-sized hail struck the Saskatoon area. Hail size varied across the city; the eastern neighbourhood of Willowgrove experienced loonie-sized hail while the downtown reported smaller hail sizes. At least 6,000 insurance claims were processed with a total of over $46 million in insured damages. Nearly half of the losses were in vehicle damages.

British Columbia and its interior and south coast regions experienced exceptionally hot and dry weather in May and throughout the summer. For 2 consecutive years, the BC wildfire seasons were record-breaking. At the end of the season, there was a reported 2,091 fires that burned over 1.35 million hectares of land; more than the previous record. A provincial State of Emergency was declared on August 15th and eventually cancelled on September 7th.

2018 was an exceptionally busy fire season in Ontario with nearly twice as many fires and more than double the burned area than the 10-year average. At the end of the season, there was a reported 1,325 fires that burned over 275,000 ha of land. In July alone, 549 fires were recorded. Over 900 out-of-province personnel were brought in from 9 provinces and territories, the United States and Mexico.

The winter of 2018 was one of the coldest on record, which created a very strong icepack throughout the Grand River watershed in Ontario. In addition to this, temperature drops led to the formation of frazil ice – heavy slush in rivers.

In early April, the deep snowpacks in parts of New Brunswick were exposed to over 48 hours of warm temperatures of up to 29C. In addition, a total of 152 mm of rain fell over a period of 31 of 32 days. Widespread flooding in the St. John River basin deeply impacted several communities including its capital of Fredericton.

Record-breaking heat was measured across Canada and in parts of southern Ontario and Quebec. A rare set of two semi-permanent highs hovered over eastern and western Canada which locked in the hot temperatures.

On September 21st, 6 tornadoes touched down in and near the National Capital Region. The strongest was an EF-3 that touched down near the City of Ottawa’s rural neighbourhoods of Kinburn and Dunrobin, and tracked almost 40 km across the Ottawa River into the lower Pontiac (Luskville) and the Mont Bleu neighbourhood of Gatineau between 4:40 pm and 5:20 pm. The estimated wind speeds were up to 265 km/hr.

A hail storm struck Calgary on July 23rd which created drifts of hail and large hailstones. The largest recorded hail stone was 64 mm in diameter – similar to the size of a tennis ball - measured in Bashaw, AB.

A severe overnight storm produced over 70 mm of rain in Toronto; some localized rainfall measured over 120 mm. The rainfall amounts ranged from +100 mm in North York and the downtown area to only 6 mm at Pearson International Airport. Several people had to be rescued from their vehicles due to the urban flooding. Flooding or flood-related water was also reported in Toronto City Hall, Scotiabank Arena, Rogers Centre, and Union Station. This overnight urban flooding event caused over $80 million in insured losses.

On May 4th, the Highway 401 corridor through southern Ontario and southern Quebec experienced a fast-moving squall line with wind gusts of over 100 km/hr. Wind speeds of 126 km/hr were recorded in Hamilton and 117 km/hr in Montreal. The windstorm caused widespread power outages, roof damage and downed trees. Over 925,000 customers across Ontario and Quebec were without power; some were without power until May 9. The windstorm caused a total of $680 million in insured losses, with at least $380 million in Ontario alone. This event is noted to be the most costly disaster in Ontario since the 2013 Toronto flood.

A large winter storm with high winds, heavy snow and ice accumulation affected parts of southern Ontario and southern Quebec. Billy Bishop Airport on Toronto Island reported winds of 96 km/hr, while Wiarton Airport reported 40 cm of snow, and London International Airport received 14 hours of freezing rain and ice pellets. Several large buildings were damaged when sheets of ice fell from neighbouring buildings – Parliament building windows were broken in Ottawa, and falling ice from the CN tower pierced the Rogers Centre Dome. Roughly 1,800 car accidents were reported including a 50-car pileup on Highway 400 near Barrie. There were over 15,000 insurance claims and $190 million in insured losses.

On June 14th severe thunderstorms affected parts of southern Manitoba. These storms generated wind gusts of over 100 km/hr and baseball-sized hail as well as a tornado near Waskada, MB. The hardest hit areas were Morden, Winkler, Ninette and Manitou, MB.
Coach bus carrying hockey team Humboldt Broncos was struck by a semi-trailer truck at the intersection of Highways 35 and 335 near Armley, SK.16 people died and 13 were injured.
Stabbing and vehicle-ramming attack near Edmonton's Commonwealth Stadium. 5 people were injured.
Vehicle-ramming attack. The perpetrator drove a rented van on the sidewalk along Yonge Street between Finch and Sheppard Avenues, hitting pedestrians. 10 people were killed and 16 injured.
Mass shooting of worshippers at the Islamic Cultural Centre of Quebec City. 6 people were killed and 5 critically  injured.
Mass shooting in Toronto's Greektown neighborhood. Three people were killed, including the perpetrator, and 13 were injured.

A powerful windstorm caused significant damage to hydro infrastructure in the Fraser Valley, the southern Gulf Island, and Vancouver Island, causing 400,000 BC Hydro customers to lose power. One person was killed in Duncan because of a falling tree.

Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302, carrying 157 passengers and crew members, crashed shortly after taking off from Addis Ababa Bole International Airport en route to Nairobi, Kenya. All 157 passengers and crew members died, including 18 Canadians. The resulting crash led to the Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft being grounded internationally over safety concerns.

From January 23rd to January 25th, 2019, a severe winter storm hit Quebec and the Maritime provinces. Over the course of the three days, heavy snowfall, freezing rain, and high winds caused over $39 million in damage, $26 million of which was in Quebec. The winter storm caused widespread school and flight cancellations, and power failures impacted 57,000 clients.
provinces: NB NL NS ON PE QC

comment: Extensive flooding in April and May was experienced across Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick due to a combination of heavy rainfalls and snow melt. In the Beauce region of Quebec, 154.5 mm of rain fell in April and was one of the first regions to be impacted by the spring floods.
provinces: NB NL NS ON PE QC

comment: Seasonal flooding along the Albany River forced the evacuation of Kashechewan First Nation, a community of 2,500, to various communities throughout Ontario including Timmins, Kapuskasing, Thunder Bay and Cornwall. The annual evacuation was moved ahead of schedule due to heavy snow.

A significant low pressure system tracked through Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia between March 14th to 16th. The winter storm produced warm temperatures and rain which caused signifncant flooding in parts of Ontario such as Bolton and Caledon along the Humber River, and in Quebec. The storm moved through Quebec and into the Maritimes on the 15th and continued to bring rain and wind. It is estimated that the storm caused $124 million in insured losses ($63 million in Quebec, $53 million in Ontario, $6.6 million in Nova Scotia, and $1.8 million in New Brunswick).
provinces: NB NL NS ON PE QC

comment: On May 22nd, a fire broke out aboard the Norwegian Bergen Line's cruise ship (the "Meteor") while returning to Vancouver after an Alaskan tour. The fire was thought to be under control until it flared up again and quickly spread below deck. The crew managed to save all the passengers, however, 32 crew members were killed and another 4 were injured in the fire.

After several inspections on the night of February 25th, a fire broke out in the early morning in the basement of a residential school in Cross Lake, MB, and quickly spread. The wing that housed the girls dormitory was only equipped with one fire escape, while the boys dormitory had two. Tragically, 12 children (11 girls, 1 boy) and 1 staff member perished in the fire.

An American Overseas Airlines flight from New York to Berlin was making its regular stop at Gander, NL, when it was diverted to the Harmon airfield (US military airfield in Stephenville, NL) due to poor weather. The Douglas DC-4 liner was serviced and took off at 5:25am (local) on October 6th in good weather conditions. A few minutes after takeoff, the aircraft crashed into Hare Mountain; only 7.5 km from the airfield runway. Of the 39 on board, there were no survivors. Hare Mountain was later renamed Crash Hill.

At 1:03 am (local) on November 1st, while several people were still celebrating Halloween festivities, a M6.1 earthquake (MMI VII) earthquake occurred 10 km east of Témiscaming, QC. It was felt as far as Thunder Bay, the Bay of Fundy, and Kentucky. Damage was reported near the epicentral region, North Bay, Mattawa and Ottawa. Most of the damage, however, was to chimneys. For example, 80% of all chimneys in Témiscaming were damaged. This earthquake also caused landslides near Lac Tee and Lac Kipawa as well as a railroad embankment failure near Parent, QC, which was roughly 300 km away. This was the largest earthquake to occur in the West Quebec Seismic Zone in historical times.

At 1:50am (local) on February 14th, a car struck a hardware store and ruptured the gas line in Essex, ON. Within minutes a gas employee had arrived to shut off the gas metre but an explosion (at 2:18am (local)) occurred before this could be done. A block of buildings including several businesses and apartments were destroyed. There were no fatalities and only 2 serious injuries. This was the second significant explosion to occur in Essex; the first being in 1907.

At 5:30pm (local), a fire broke out and quickly destroyed a 2-storey Roman Catholic mission hospital in Alexis Creek, BC - located on the Anahim Reserve. Tragically, 12 indigenous children were killed - all under the age of 9 years. One child was rescued but the nun who performed the rescue suffered severe burns.

At 6:30pm (local) on December 9th, there was an explosion at the West Canadian Collieries No. 1 mine in Bellevue, AB, which trapped 47 miners underground. The mine had no rescue training or equipment and relied on a mine rescue team from Fernie B.C's Hosmer mine for help. Thirty-one miners were killed; 21 of these deaths, including one member of the mine rescue team, were due to "after damp”, a deadly mix of carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide.

At 9:19 pm (local) on February 28th, an M6.2 earthquake (MMI VIII) occurred near Ile aux Lievres, QC, in the St. Lawrence River. The earthquake was one of the largest to have occurred in eastern Canada in historical times and was felt over 1,000 km away. Damage occurred on both the north and south shores of the St. Lawrence and in at least 14 communities including Baie-St-Paul, La Malbaie, Ste-Anne-de-la-Pocatiere and Riviere Ouelle. Damage ranged from out-of-plane failures of bricks, thrown down chimneys, dislodged stones (especially in churches), cracked masonry, and fallen or overturned building content. Damage was noted as far as Quebec City, Trois-Rivieres, Shawinigan, northern New Brunswick and Ottawa. Six individuals suffered fatal heart attacks as a result of the earthquake.

At about 8:00pm (local) on February 14th, a fire broke out on the fifth floor of the Crèche d'Youville (Grey Nuns Orphanage) in Montreal, QC, which housed an orphanage. Firefighters and convalescing soldiers aided in the rescue efforts. Sadly, 53 children perished in the fire.

On April 17th, the "Flora Alberta" - a 42.5 m (140 ft.) long fishing schooner left Lunenburg, NS, with a crew of 28. As a convoy of 8 ships including the steamer "Fanad Head" (128 m / 420 ft. long) left Halifax, NS, en route to the United Kingdom. By 2:00am (local) on the 21st, a dense fog caused very poor visibility, and at 5:20am the Flora Alberta and the Fanad Head collided. The small fishing schooner was torn in half and sank within minutes. Only 11 out of the crew of 28 survived.
In June of 1903, a wildfire burned the community of Hopewell Cape, NB, including the courthouse and 21 other buildings.

In June of 1908, Old Man River in Alberta experienced one of its highest peak flows in history; caused by heavy rains and an already saturated ground because of snowmelt. On June 6th, the peak flow was estimated to be 200,000 cubic feet per second (cfs) , and 8 m (26.7 ft.) above normal river levels. Due to the floods of 1902, the river had widened, therefore the flood of 1908 had a higher volume of water but a slightly less height above normal. Regardless, the 1908 flood caused significant losses to several communities such as Lethbridge and McLeod, AB. This included a population dip in Lethbridge, significant damage to critical infrastructure  (e.g. damage to the new CPR bridge, viaduct, powerhouse, and hospital), and the destruction of many homes.

In June of 1953, the Old Man River in Alberta experienced another  significant flooding event. The recorded peak flow was 110,000 cubic feet per second (cfs) and 7m (23.1 ft.) above normal river levels. The community power plant closed for a week, and the water supply was temporarily halved, causing over 150 individuals to be evacuated. As a result of this flood, Lethbridge rezoned the residential area in the floodplain to parkland (now Indian Battle Park), and encouraged several residents to relocate outside of the floodplain.

On August 4th, a moderately severe geomagnetic storm caused disruptions in communication and power services throughout Canada and the United States. In Canada, power disturbances were noted at the Newfoundland and Labrador Power Commission, Hydro-Quebec, Ontario Hydro, and Manitoba Hydro.
provinces: AB BC MB NB NL NT NS NU ON PE QC SK YT

comment: In the afternoon of June 27th, three tornadoes touched down in a severe thunderstorm that tracked from Quebec and into Ontario. The first tornado (F1) touched down at 3:20pm (local) by Thorn Lake and caused an 11 km path of damage to Lac-des-Loups. The second tornado (F3) touched down at 3:45pm near Cascades, QC, and caused a 60 km path of damage to Pendleton, ON. The last tornado (F2) touched down at 5:10pm near Bernardin, ON, and caused a 14 km path of damage. Although these tornadoes were typical in formation, duration, direction, etc., they did display unique characteristics in rough terrain (e.g., increasing in intensity on the downslope and valleys). The second and largest tornado impacted the community of Masson-Anger, QC, and damaged 50 houses and businesses, injuring 36 individuals. The damage is estimated to be $3-$4 million (CAD 1979).

In the afternoon of October 25th, a faulty gas line exploded near the intersection of Airport and Derry Roads (the Four Corners) in Malton, ON. Nine businesses were destroyed; many were never rebuilt. Several families also lost their homes in addition to hundreds who were evacuated. The fire killed 1 resident, and injured 22 others.

In the early afternoon of December 21st, a 35-tonne dump truck carrying a load of sand overturned at an intersection onto a school bus full of children near Oldcastle, ON, (within the City of Windsor). Tragically, 8 children between the ages of 6 and 9 lost their lives, a further 16 others were sustained injuries. At the time, this was considered the worst traffic accident in Windsor-area history.

In the early afternoon of June 25th, a 10-car passenger train (the Winnipeg Express) bound for the Prairies carrying newly arrived immigrants from Ireland and Scotland, left the Ottawa train station. At McKellar town site (now the McKellar Park neighbourhood in Ottawa), several train cars left the track and toppled into the Ottawa River. The train accident resulted in 8 deaths and injured at least 50 others.

In the early hours of April 27th, a bus carrying 42 music students and 7 chaperones from Newton, Massachusetts, overturned near Sussex, NB. Sadly, 4 students were killed, while another 37 passengers were injured, including 11 with serious injuries.

In the early hours of April 29th, a fire started in a stairwell of the Rossmore hotel in Cornwall, ON. At the time, there were about 60 guests in addition to staff in the hotel. Because the fire was accidentally started on the stairwell between the first 2 floors, this created a barrier for escape, and many guests jumped or climbed out of windows. Sadly, 10 individuals perished in the fire, while others sustained injuries from their burns or from jumping out of the hotel’s windows. The fire also destroyed several other businesses including the telegraph office, a jewelry store and the telephone company. The damage was estimated to be $250,000 (1910 CAD).

During the last week of May, the temperatures soared to over 30 Celsius causing snowmelt and flooding conditions across BC, the Yukon and Alaska. The Skeena, Columbia and Thompson Rivers reached record levels. The Skeena River changed its course in several places including Terrace, BC, which led to severe erosion—for instance, one farm lost 4.8 ha in 3 days. The communities of Usk and Remo were significantly impacted. In Usk, the flood waters were 1.8-3 m high and only 3 buildings in the community were not damaged. In Remo, the water was 2.4 m, and only 1 house was not damaged. The Skeena River also carved new river channels including one through the community of Kispiox, and with it, 20 buildings. Several infrastructure was damaged including hundreds of meters of rail lines, at least 22 bridges, community powerhouses, 10 km of telephone and telegraph lines, kilometers of roadways and ferry infrastructure. Damage to roads, bridges and ferry infrastructure was $35,100 (CAD 1916); $21,305 alone was in the Terrace-Kitwanga area.

In the early morning hours of September 15th, Hurricane Hortense made landfall near Sheet Harbour, NS— the first hurricane to made landfall in Nova Scotia in 21 years. At landfall, Hortense was a category 1 hurricane with winds near 120 km/hr. Hortense quickly downgraded to a tropical storm, and transitioned to a post-tropical storm to the south of Newfoundland by the afternoon of the 15th. The maximum recorded wind speed was 161 km/hr near St. Paul Island in the Cabot Strait, the maximum rainfall was 95-137.5 mm, there were 8 m waves near the Halifax Harbour as well as a 0.75 m storm surge were recorded in or near Halifax (it was over 1m east of Halifax). Hortense caused numerous power outages, damage to windows and roofs as well as flooding. The total property losses were almost $5 million.
In the early hours of December 4th, the "SS Lunenburg" ran aground near the Iles-de-la-Madeleine, QC. Of the 17 crew and passenger aboard, 11 lives were lost.

In the early hours of February 6th, a Trans-Canada Air Lines flight from Montreal, QC, to Winnipeg, MB, reported an engine issue after taking off from North Bay, ON, and was diverted to Armstrong airport for an emergency landing in northern Ontario. When the aircraft failed to land, rescue plans were initiated. Later in the morning, the wreckage was found roughly 1.5 kilometres from the airport. None of the 12 individuals on board survived.

In the early hours of January 19th, a Northwest Airlines DC-4 crashed while making an emergency landing at Sandspit, BC. The flight between Tokyo, Japan, to Washington State had encountered a mechanical issue and attempted to land at Sandspit airport during a winter storm, but crashed into the water just over a kilometre offshore. Of the 43 crew and military passengers on-board, many survived the crash itself but succumbed to exposure; there were only 7 survivors.

In the early hours of May 4th, a fire broke out beside Spencer's Opera House in Sandon, BC. The fire spread so quickly that fire-fighting equipment had to be abandoned. Furthermore, 2 years earlier, Carpenter's Creek was covered by a boardwalk leaving it inaccessible for water and fire suppression efforts. A firebreak was successfully created by dynamite which saved a part of the town. Also a concerted and successful effort was made to save the livery barn filled with horses. There was only 1 fatality and $750,000 (1900 CAD) in losses - 10 hotels, a bank, several local businesses, 2 churches and numerous homes were destroyed leaving most of the town homeless (estimated 1,200 individuals).

In the early hours of October 25th, the steamer "Hestia" ran aground on Proprietor Ledge near Grand Manan, NB. Of the 40 crew and passengers on board, there were only 6 survivors. All of those in the lifeboats perished, while the 6 who stayed aboard survived.

In the early hours of September 9th, a small fire started behind a business in Hebertville-Station, QC, but a strong wind spread the fire to the neighbouring church. With strong winds and poor access to water, the fire spread across the community. By 5:00am, 20 businesses including; the bank, jewelry store, town hall, train station and 2 hotels as well as 35 other buildings were destroyed. While there were no deaths, and only a few injuries, 20 families (roughly 175 individuals) became homeless. Furthermore, the losses were estimated to be $300,000 (1930 CAD); of which $85,000 of which was insured.

On March 24th, a geomagnetic storm created communication interruptions in most overseas radio-telephone lines, service to ships at sea, and telephone landlines. The most significant disruptions occurred over a 6 hour period but some disturbances to overseas services (especially the transatlantic services) persisted for several days. In Canada and the United States, the Eastern Seaboard was more affected than other places. This storm was also the first time that the effects of space weather was reported on power systems. Disruptions to the power systems were most notable in Ontario and Quebec.
provinces: AB BC MB NB NL NT NS NU ON PE QC SK YT

comment: In the early morning of August 8th, the "George A. Marsh", a coal schooner from Belleville, ON, encountered strong winds near Simcoe Island, ON, and sank. Of the 14 crew and passengers including several children, there were only 2 survivors.

In the early morning of May 7th, the "HMCS Valleyfield" was travelling in a convoy of 5 naval ships returning from overseas to St. John's, NL, was torpedoed by a German U-boat. The HMCS Valleyfield was hit on its port side - near the boiler room - which caused a large explosion. The ship sank in less than 5 minutes. Of the 163 officers and crew aboard, 125 perished either in the explosion or in the cold waters.

In the late afternoon of May 8th, a small brush fire spread to the General Explosive Company factory in Hull, QC. It is reported that at the time, about 2,000 spectators were gathered nearby to watch a baseball game; many of whom left the game to watch the fire. After a series of small explosions, there were 2 large explosions that detonated about 4 tons of explosives. Roughly 30 buildings were destroyed in Hull, and thousands of windows were blown out in both Hull and Ottawa; the explosion was felt as far away as 16 km. The explosions killed 11 individuals including children and injured 37 others.

In the spring of 1904, Lumsden, SK, had "the year of the great flood". The Qu'Appelle River that runs through the community, overflowed its banks. Almost all the houses were impacted and train service was disrupted. For residents, a floating sidewalk was installed. Additionally, the road leading up to the bridge was flooded, so homesteaders passing through along the 'trail' had to stay in tents for 2 weeks waiting for the water to recede.

Just after 2:00am (local) on November 25th, the St. Boniface College - a Jesuit boarding school - caught fire. The school, built in 1882, housed 195 staff and students as well as a large collection of historical artifacts and documents. Many students and staff were instrumental in the rescue efforts,  9 students (mostly under the age of 16) and one clergyman perished in the fire, with a further 18 sustaining injuries. The collection of historical items were also destroyed.

Just after midnight (local) on September 5th, an M5.8 earthquake (MMI VIII) occurred near the Ontario-New York border. The earthquake was felt over much of eastern Ontario, southern Quebec and the New England states. The most significant damage was to chimneys. In Cornwall for example, roughly 2,000 chimneys were damaged. An out-of-plane failure at Cornwall Collegiate and Vocational School fell from the upper level, through the gymnasium roof and onto the floor - luckily the earthquake occurred outside of school hours. Damage is estimated to be between $600,000 and $1 million (CAD 1944).

Just after midnight on December 8th, a fire was accidently started by a kitchen assistant at the Barry Hotel in Saskatoon, SK. The fire quickly spread from the open lobby and up the 3 storeys of the hotel. Within an hour, 11 individuals were killed and 18 were injured - several from jumping or climbing from the windows.

Just after midnight on May 24th, an arsonist set fire to the Moose Hall in Hamilton, ON, during a dance for Royal Oak Dairy employees. Most of the attendees were trapped on the second floor and jumped from the windows. Sadly, there were 10 fatalities, and 47 individuals who were injured. Consequently, 12 children were orphaned. This fire is known to be the deadliest fire in Hamilton's history.

Just before noon on June 22nd, a fire was accidentally lit behind a family home and quickly spread out-of-control in Trois-Rivières, QC. Special trains with fire crews and equipment were brought in from Montreal, Quebec City, Sherbrooke and Grande Mere to help in the efforts. In the end, 800 buildings were destroyed including a significant portion of the business district. Some of these buildings included City Hall, the post office, several high-end hotels, a bank, the oldest Anglican church in Canada, and several other businesses as well as 215 homes. Although there were no reported deaths, there were 3 individuals who sustained injuries. The property losses are estimated to be $1 million (1908 CAD).

On April 12th at 2:24 pm (local), a VIA rail passenger train derailed near Stewiacke, NS. After a Canadian National rail switch was tampered with, 9 train cars derailed into an adjacent farm supply building; destroying both the building and track. Of the 132 individuals on the train, 22 were injured, 9 of which had serious injuries.
On October 31st, a geomagnetic storm that lasted for 8 hours created significant disruptions to the telegraph, telephone and cable systems around the world.
provinces: AB BC MB NB NL NT NS NU ON PE QC SK YT

comment: On April 19th, while following five bulk freighters through the Sault locks, the "S.S.Lambton" - a government-owned lighthouse steamer - damaged its steering gear. It was last seen in strong gales near Caribou Island; wreckage was reported on April 24th. All 21 individuals, including 16 crew and 5 lighthouse keepers perished.

On April 25th at around 10:30am (local) and just 6 minutes after take-off, a Liberator bomber lost altitude and crashed in two apartment houses on Shannon Street (south of Ottawa Street) in downtown Montreal. Since the aircraft's fuel tanks were full (9,000 L of fuel), there was an explosion and fire that further destroyed 15 other homes. The air accident caused 15 deaths, 5 of which were the crew.

On April 28th, a Trans-Canada Air Lines flight from Lethbridge, AB, to Vancouver, BC, went missing near Vancouver. The wreckage was not found until  September of 1994. All 15 individuals on-board perished in the air accident.

On April 7th, a meeting in support of native rule in Portugal's African territories at the University of Toronto was interrupted when an opposing group shattered glass doors and overturned tables. The meeting was attended by roughly 250 people where 56 were injured.

On August 10th at 9:50am (local), a boxcar loaded with 5,000 lbs of nitro-glycerin exploded near the Essex Railway Station in Essex, ON. The explosives were being shipped by rail to Amherstburg, via Essex, to help dredge the Detroit River. In the heat of the August morning, the dynamite/nitro-glycerin began to melt and drip through the floor of the car onto the tracks when the shunting trains ignited them. Two rail workers were killed in the blast which left a 6 m by 3 m crater. A church, 2 mills, the electricity plant, several industrial facilities and homes were destroyed, while nearly every building in the community was damaged. Several individuals were injured. The damage was estimated to be $250,000 (1907 CAD).

On August 10th, a fire broke out in the Mystic Rill and Scenic Railway rides at Dominion Park in Montreal. The fire collapsed the Scenic Railway ride into Mystic Rill which was a winding watercourse ride with small boats. As a result, 7 individuals perished.
On August 10th, a fire burned a city block containing 40 homes in Hull, QC, leaving 200 homeless.

On August 12th, a significant hail event impacted Calgary and its surrounding area. Hailstones as large as golf balls damaged vehicles, windows, gardens and trees as well as the iconic Calgary Saddledome. The hail event led to over half a billion dollars in insured losses (2012 dollars).

On August 20th just after midnight, two Orthodox Doukhobor communal settlements (Gelboff and Chevaldave) in the village of Ootechenia were destroyed by arson-related fires. In total, 26 homes and buildings were destroyed leaving 60 homeless. The arsonists also damaged the community's water pump which inhibited fire suppression efforts. The losses were estimated to be $100,000 (1961 CAD).

On September 25th, a geomagnetic storm created significant telegraphic disturbances around the world including transatlantic cables. Auroras were reported in Singapore which was the lower latitude ever reported.
provinces: AB BC MB NB NL NT NS NU ON PE QC SK YT

comment: On August 21st, the tug "C.C. Martin" was towing the barge "Albatross" during a strong gale (wind storm) near Key Harbour, ON (Georgian Bay and the French River). The Albatross took on water and foundered - which also took the tug C.C. Martin down with it. While those on the Albatross survived, all 10 crew members and passenger on the tug perished.

On August 2nd, Air France flight 358 from Paris to Toronto carrying 297 passengers and 12 crew members on board was preparing to land at Toronto's Pearson airport during a thunderstorm at 4:02pm (local) in the afternoon. During the landing, there was heavy rain, poor visibility and lightning strikes. The aircraft was not able to stop before the end of the 2.7 km long runway, crashed in the ravine adjacent to the runway and caught fire. All 309 individuals successfully evacuated the aircraft. In total, 33 individuals were taken to hospital, 21 of those had minor injuries and 12 had serious injuries.

On August 3rd at 5:09am (local), a Canadian National freight train derailed near Wabamun, AB. Of the 3 locomotives and 140 cars, a total of 43 derailed including 1 loaded with pole treating oil, 1 loaded with toluene, and 25 loaded with heavy fuel oil. Roughly 700,000 L of heavy fuel oil, and 88,000 L of pole treating oil were spilled. The derailment affected a 1 km2 land area; some of the spilled material penetrated into the groundwater, and some ended up in Lake Wabamun. Water advisories (including drinking, swimming, fishing and boating) were put in place after the spill and were gradually lifted throughout August and September. While there were no short-term impacts on fish, however, submerged oil did negatively impact waterfowl throughout the following year.

place: Lower Mainland and Vancouver Island, British Columbia
comment: From January 19-29, a significant cold event impacted BC's Lower Mainland and Vancouver Island where temperatures dropped to -16C. The cold event created fuel shortages as well as frozen water supplies. On January 21st, the roof of the Hastings Park Forum (the city's main hockey and curling rink) collapsed after 43 cm of snow fell. This event was followed by a 4-day rain event that dropped 267 mm of rain which further caused widespread and extensive roof damage in the impacted area.

On August 5th at 6:24am (local), a Canadian National freight train derailed near Garibaldi, BC. The freight train consisted of 7 locomotives, 141 empty cars and 3 cars loaded with sodium hydroxide. The derailment occurred on the Cheakamus River bridge. While only 9 cars derailed, 4 of those had fallen off the bridge including 1 carrying sodium hydroxide. Roughly 40,000 L of sodium hydroxide spilled onto the surrounding rocks and into the Cheakamus River. The fast-moving waters in Cheakamus River Canyon carried the spilled sodium hydroxide solution downstream which quickly affected aquatic life both in the Cheakamus River and lower Squamish River. The spill killed fish as well as benthic invertebrates; Provincial and Federal reports calculated that 500,000 fish from 10 different species died as a result of the spill.

On August 7th, a hurricane transitioned to a post-tropical storm in Atlantic Canada where the winds were estimated to be between 140-150 km/hr. The Lunenburg schooners - the "Sylvia Mosher" and the "Sadie S. Knickle" - were lost with all 49 of their crews, with some of debris washing ashore on Sable Island.

After running aground near Anticosti Island, QC, the tanker "Cymbeline" was undergoing repairs in dry dock at the Port of Montreal. On June 17th at 3:55am (local), when the night maintenance crew were working on the damaged tanker, a large explosion occurred. As the firefighters arrived to assess the scene, a second and more powerful explosion occurred. The resulting fire continued to burn for 14 hours. As a result of the explosions and fire, 30 individuals including the fire chief and 3 firefighters were killed, while another 35 were seriously injured.
On August 9th, an explosion at the Michel Colliery in Michel, BC, killed 13 miners. The blast also damaged other buildings in the community, including the mine, the school, and local businesses.

On Christmas night at 9:31 pm (local), 2 passenger trains, the Toronto-Detroit express and an excursion train, collided near Dundas Station, ON, (now Hamilton). It is believed that an open switch led the fast-moving express onto the track where the excursion train was stationary. In the collision, 15 were killed and another 45 were injured.

place: Mollie Gibson Mine, Kokanee Lake, British Columbia
comment: On Christmas night, an avalanche destroyed most of the buildings at the Mollie Gibson Mine located north of Kokanee Landing, BC (near Kokanee Creek Provincial Park). Of the 19 men in the bunkhouse, 9 were killed and at least 1 was severely injured. The avalanche also blocked the mine entrance and 4 men were stranded in the No. 5 tunnel.
On December 10th, a United States Air Force DC-4 crashed near Goose Bay, NL. Of the 29 individuals on board, 23 were killed in the crash.

On December 11th at around 10:00am (local), a spark in the warehouse set off a series of fires and explosions at the Quaker Oats plant in Peterborough, ON. The fire killed 24 individuals and injured several others. At the time, the plant played a significant role in the war effort, and extraordinary measures were made to reduce hardship to employees and rebuild.

On December 12th, at a level-crossing on St. Clair Avenue E. and the GO train crossing, a malfunction on a TTC bus left it stranded on the tracks. As the GO Train approached the crossing and the bus unable to move, panic-stricken bus passengers attempted to exit the bus as quickly as possible. Sadly, there was not enough time to evacuate the entire bus before it was struck by the GO Train; 10 bus passengers were killed and another 20 were injured. This was considered to be the worst transit disaster in Toronto's history.

On December 14th at around 10:30pm (local) a fire broke out in Hospice St. Charles—a reform school and orphanage in Quebec City. While there are mixed reports of the number of fatalities, estimates for the death toll range between 31 and 37 children.
On December 20th, a Canadian Pacific Airlines flight from Prince George, BC, to Vancouver, BC, crashed into the Cheam Range in poor weather. All 13 individuals on board were killed.
On December 25th, the Schooner "Tiber" foundered off Canso, NS. All 21 lives on board were lost.

On December 26th, a fire broke out in the basement of Stedman's Store in Springhill, NS, and quickly spread to surrounding buildings due to high winds. Suppression efforts were further compounded when a power outage affected the water pressure. The fire spread down Main Street and destroyed 14 businesses, 4 houses and 10 apartments. While there were no fatalities and only a few minor injuries, 34 residents were left homeless.

On December 30th, the Swift Current Broncos were travelling on their team bus to Regina for a Western Hockey League hockey game. In poor weather conditions, the bus lost control on black ice, left the overpass, and came to a rest on its side. Of the 28 players, staff and driver on-board, 4 were killed and 19 were injured.

On December 6th, a lone gunman entered École Polytechnique and killed 14 women and injured 14 others. During the shooting, the gunman targeted women by separating them from the men, and shouted "I hate feminists". The gunman then took his own life.

On December 8th, the first of three avalanches released in the Harvey Pass area (40 km south of Fernie, BC) and buried a group of seven snowmobilers. Another group of snowmobilers heard the yelling and joined in the rescued efforts. As they were digging out the last victim, a second avalanche released; burying the entire group. Two individuals dug themselves out, and rescued another. A third avalanche was reported, but only depositing some powder. Of the 11 snowmobilers involved, 8 perished.

On February 11th, a series of avalanches released above McLean Point along the shore of the Skeena River. At the time, there was a construction camp along the river to house workers building the highway between Prince Rupert and Terrace, BC. In the days leading up to the avalanche, a storm dropped rain that changed to snow at the camp. At 7:30am (local) on the 11th, the first of three avalanches impacted the camp. Two bunkhouses and the first aid shack were destroyed. Soon thereafter, the second avalanche struck, and destroyed most of the camp leaving only two buildings standing. Twenty minutes later, a third avalanche occurred, and destroyed the construction office. Three individuals were killed and 11 were severely injured. Ten years prior to this event, a snow shed covering the rail tracks was destroyed by an avalanche at the same location. This fact was overlooked by the highway construction managers who sited the camp at the same location.

On February 13th at 2:48pm (local), Le Front de Libération du Québec (FLQ) network bombed the Montreal Stock Exchange. The time bomb comprised of at least 6 sticks of dynamite and 2 of Pento-mex. Although there was a telephone warning 3 minutes before the detonation, there was not enough time to evacuate. Of the 300 persons in the building, 27 were injured, 3 of them seriously. Furthermore, there was a total of $1 million (1969 CAD) in damages. In February of 1969, the FLQ carried out, or attempted to carry out, at least 8 domestic terrorist bomb attacks in Montreal.
On February 9th, 2 passenger trains collided head-on near Sand Point, ON. As a result, 13 individuals were killed and another 19 were injured.
On January 10th, a fire broke out at the Monte Carlo Theatre in Dawson City, YT, which burned down a large section of the community's business district.

On January 12th, a passenger van carrying the Bathurst High School basketball team lost control and collided with an oncoming truck near Bathurst, NB. Sadly, 7 players and a teacher were killed in the accident; the other 4 passengers sustained injuries.

On January 14th, a Northern Thunderbird Air flight from Prince George, BC, crashed on approach to the Terrace, BC, airport in a winter storm. The crash claimed the lives of all 12 individuals on board.
On January 14th, an explosion at the Hamilton Powder Company killed 12 employees in Departure Bay, BC.

On January 17th, a Cessna Caravan departed Pelee Island airport at 4:38pm (local) carrying 9 passengers and the pilot. However, at 7:08pm, the United States Coast Guard spotted wreckage 3 km from the end of the runway. Although the weather conditions were poor at the time, the accident was attributed to a 15% weight exceedance and ice contamination on the aircraft. All 10 individuals and 2 hunting dogs were killed in the accident.

On January 18th at 1:15am (local), a fire broke out at the Haslemere Apartments—a 3-storey apartment block containing 28 units. Many residents were unable to evacuate the building, leaving them no choice but to jump from their windows. Twenty-two residents were taken to the hospital, of those 6 people were hospitalized, with most sustaining injuries from jumping or falling from the building. Three firefighters were also injured while putting out the fires which ultimately caused the deaths of 9 residents. As a result of this apartment fire, recommendations were made regarding fire safety in older apartment buildings which were adopted in August of 1975.

On January 18th at around 2:00am (local), a fire broke out at the College of the Sacred Heart in St-Hyacinthe, QC. At least 45 students and staff perished in the fire in addition to 21 others who were injured.

On January 23rd at around 7:30pm (local), a fire broke out on rue Saint-Pierre in Montreal, QC. When the first warehouse collapsed, it started several other small fires which spread to the south and east. In the end, the fire destroyed a few blocks of Montreal's business sector. About 30 buildings were destroyed including the Board of Trade. Some reports estimate the damage to be $5 million (1901 CAD).

On January 30th at 10:12am (local), a VIA rail passenger train was diverted to the incorrect track and collided with 11 stationary cars. Both locomotives and 7 passenger cars derailed, sending 43 of the 127 individuals on board to hospital, 8 of which had serious injuries.

On January 8th, the passenger steamer "SS Clallam" left Port Townsend, Washington, en route to Victoria, BC. The Clallam was carrying 92 passengers and crew when it encountered a storm in the Salish Sea in the afternoon. As the storm intensified, the SS Clallam began to take on water. Tugs were sent from Vancouver Island and other nearby locations to assist the steamer . Of the 92 individuals on board, there were only 36 survivors. It is reported that no women and children survived as the lifeboats they were in overturned before the tugs arrived. In the early hours of January 9th, the SS Clallam sank.

On July 14, a large rain storm settled in near Peterborough, ON. In the early hours of July 15, over 235 mm of rain fell – which was typically a summer's worth of rain in the region. It was one of the wettest days in Ontario's history, and the rain continued for the next 5 days. There was extensive flooding in Peterborough; most of the downtown area and a third of the city was flooded under a metre of water. The wastewater system was at 5 times the capacity leading to backed up sewers. A State of Emergency was declared and in effect for 15 days. Clean-up efforts took months, while some of the city’s infrastructure needed to be rebuilt. The Province of Ontario provided $25 million for emergency repair and restoration of municipal infrastructure, the insured losses were over $83 million (CAD 2004).

On July 15th, an explosion occurred at a coal mine near Cumberland, BC. Reports indicate that between 12 and 21 individuals were killed (one report noted that 15 Chinese workers were killed) in the explosion and another 8 were injured.

On July 16th, a mini-bus carrying seniors collided with a van and caught fire between La Tuque and Roberval, QC, along route 155. Of the 19 individuals in the mini-bus, only 2 survived—both with significant burn injuries. The 2 passengers of the van were also killed in the accident.

On July 16th, Reid's Crystal Hall, a 3 storey brick building undergoing renovations in London, ON, collapsed. The building came down onto the sidewalk and adjacent buildings trapping several individuals. As a result of the collapse, 7 were killed while 40 were injured.

On August 21st, an aircraft flying from Churchill, MB, to Winnipeg crashed near Bigstone Lake in northern Manitoba. There were 21 individuals on-board including the crew, a meteorological team, a reporter, a physiotherapist and 8 Indigenous people. Sadly, there were no survivors.

On July 23rd, Victoria experienced its first "Great Fire" where five city blocks burned in a matter of 4 hours. The fire began at the Albion Iron Works. The aftermath included the destruction of over 100 homes leaving 250 people homeless.

On July 24th, a chartered flight for the Consolidated Paper Company was flying from Anticosti, QC, to Gaspé crashed near Cap-des-Rosier, QC. On approach to Gaspé, the aircraft crashed into the hills at Cap-Bon-Ami which were concealed by fog. Of the 26 individuals on board, there were no survivors.

On July 2nd at around 4:00am (local), a fire started at a Chinese restaurant in Cobalt, ON, and quickly spread. Because of the nature of this frontier town, it was built without municipal water nor sewer infrastructure which impeded suppression efforts. In the end, approximately 150 buildings burned and 3,000 were left homeless. There were reports of 2 fatalities and 6 injuries.

On July 30th, a fire was accidentally initiated in the Lower North Thompson Valley. In August, a state of emergency was declared on the 1st, and 3,800 residents  were evacuated from Barriere, McLure, and Louis Creek, BC. Because the main highway was closed, the evacuations had to be via ferry or on a route that climbed 1,311 m in elevation. Up to this date, BC had an exceptional fire season with 189 fires burning at the same time. Since fire response resources were stretched across the province, out-of-province and military personnel were brought in to help in the fire effort. The Canadian Armed Forces 'Operation Peregrine' provided firefighting assistance for 45 days from early August to October 5th; roughly 400 personnel assisted with the McClure fire. By August 27th, 1,079 firefighters were fighting the fire. The fire lasted for over 75 days, burned 26,240 ha (262 km2) including 72 homes and 9 businesses. The losses were estimated to be $31 million (CAD 2005) and $8.2 million in property damage. Additionally, the loss of a sawmill in Louis Creek led to the more than 180 employees permanently losing their jobs. In British Columbia, the insured losses of this fire season were $200 million (2003 CAD).

On June 11th, a group of 27 school children and 4 adult leaders from St. John's Private School were on year end school canoe trip on Lake Timiskaming, ON, when the winds capsized their canoes. Sadly, 12 children and 1 adult lost their lives.

On June 13th, a 37,850 L (10,000 gal) water tank collapsed on the roof and through most of the floors of The Herald newspaper building in Montreal, QC. As a result, a fire also started in the building. In the end, 32 individuals were killed, mostly by the collapse of the water tank, and a further 50 sustained injuries.

On June 13th, the small community of Faro, YT, was affected by 2 fires. Reports note that the first fire was initiated at around midnight, but was under control by mid-afternoon. The second fire was initiated by lightning near the community of Pelly Crossing, YT, - 4 km northwest of Faro. The community of Faro began as a mining camp and construction had begun on the town site in Fall of 1968. During that night, part of the mining camp, the construction camp and the partly finished community burned down. Pelly Crossing was evacuated, but was not destroyed by the fire. In the end, the burned area measured 73,000 ha (730 km2) causing the destruction of 50 buildings in Faro, costing an estimated $500,000 (1969 CAD).

On June 15th at around noon (local), a fire broke out in an elevator shaft on the third floor of the Sainte-Cunegonde hospice in Montreal. The fire quickly spread to the upper floors and it took firefighters 4 hours to get it under control. Sadly, 35 individuals perished in the fire.

On June 17th, an EF2 tornado struck Angus, ON, a community 18 km southwest of Barrie. At 5:00pm (local), a line of severe thunderstorms moved into the region and within 15 minutes, the tornado tracked through the community of Angus. The tornado was on the ground for 20 km and damaged 102 homes, 14 of which were beyond repair. The tornado left 300 individuals homeless, caused 3 minor injuries and over $50 million (CAD 2014) in insured losses. A state of emergency was in place for a week.

On June 1st, a bus carrying 44 passengers veered off the road and down a ravine near Saint-Joseph-de-la-Rive, QC. Of the 44 passengers on board, 14 were fatally injured. In 1997, a similar bus accident occurred at the same location.

On June 20th, a fire broke out near a drying kiln at the Knight Bros. Co. Sash and Door Factory in Burk's Falls, ON. The fire quickly spread to Ontario Street and burned most of the downtown area. The fires destroyed 25 businesses, as well as a church and 5 homes, while several other homes were damaged. There is a report of 1 injury, while many were left homeless. There was $150,000 (1908 CAD) in property damage, of which only $70,000 (1908 CAD) was insured.

On June 23rd, shortly after taking off from Port Hardy, BC, the pilot of an Pacific Western Airlines DC-3 requested permission to land due to the 'feel of the aircraft'. Sadly, the aircraft crash landed. Of the 18 on-board, there were only 4 survivors.

On June 25th at 1:32pm (local), an explosion occurred in the basement of a garage in Montreal, QC. After firefighters and onlookers arrived, a second explosion occurred at 2:07pm which blew out the façade of two of the garage's floors. As a result of this explosion, 3 firefighters were killed and another died as a result of their injuries, while a further 97 others were injured.

On June 2nd, a wildfire (the Whisp fire) was reported north of Fort John near Whispering Pines Lake, BC. After an inspection, it was decided to let the 80 ha fire burn freely. According to the policy at the time, fire crews were not allowed to suppress fires until they were within a certain distance of a road, community or major river. Even though local Metis trappers volunteered to help suppress the fire as it moved towards and into Alberta, fire crews were ordered not to go. A second fire began on July 29th, and eventually joined the Whisp fire between September 20 and 22nd. By this time, there were over 30 fires greater than 200 ha burning along the northern borders of BC and Alberta; the newly-merged Chinchaga fire spread 63 km. The smoke plume drifted from northern Alberta to southern Ontario which caused high mid-day electricity demand to turn on the lights and subsequently led to several power outages. The Whisp/Chinchaga fires burned 1.4 million ha (14,000 km2) and was recorded as the largest wildfire in North American history. The majority of the burned area was in Alberta; only 90,000 ha were in BC.
On June 3rd, a fire burned a city block containing 35 homes in Hull, QC. Now, the block is home to parc Ste-Bernadette.

On June 4th, the community of Saint-Victor, QC, was affected by another fire (1916, 1931). The fire destroyed 33 houses, a convent-boarding school, and 60 other outbuildings. As a result, over 200 individuals lost their homes.

On June 8th, a small bonfire quickly became out-of-control and burned a significant part of Saint-Victor-de-Tring, QC, (now Saint-Victor) including 29 homes, the convent, and 50 other outbuildings. The community had also been affected by a major fire in 1913 and then another in 1948.

On June 8th, at 1:18am (local), the Winnipeg fire department responded to a call of a small fire behind a neon sign at the Time Building—a 7-storey building near Portage Avenue and Hargrave Street. Due to strong winds, the fire spread, and by 5:53am, it had jumped Hargrave Street and burned the Dismorr Block and onto The Henry Building. All firetrucks in the department (except 2) were dispatched to the large fire, which was eventually contained by the end of the morning. In the end, the fire destroyed over 100 businesses and caused an estimated $2-$3 million (1954 CAD) in losses in addition to almost $35,000 in municipal costs (demolition, fire equipment). This event is considered to be one of the worst fires in Winnipeg's history.
On June 9th, a bus carrying seniors lost control during a rainstorm and crashed into an overpass near Sainte-Rosalie, QC. As a result, 11 seniors were killed and another 20 were injured.
On Labour Day weekend, a 3 vehicle accident involving 2 trucks and bus occurred near Lantzville, BC,  resulting in the death of 10 individuals.

On March 12th at 9:55am (local), a Cougar Helicopter (Cougar 91) crashed off the coast of Newfoundland while on route to the Hibernia oil platform. The helicopter, which was carrying of 2 crew and 16 passengers, had an issue with its main gearbox oil pressure and was diverted back to St John's airport. Within 20 minutes, it had crashed - all but 1 individual were killed in the crash.

On March 14th at 1:40pm (local), an Ontario Northland Railway freight train derailed near Temagami, ON. Of the 29 cars that derailed, 25 contained sulphuric acid. Approximately 386,000 liters of sulphuric acid spilled into the surrounding environment 144,000 liters entered Martin Creek with 35,000 liters migrating to Hornet Lake. One month after the accident, the pH at the bottom of Hornet Lake measured 2.5 and further remediation/treatment took place to neutralize the water. Bottom dwelling lake organisms and fish were impacted near the derailment site.

On March 16th, a van carrying 10 daycare children collided with another vehicle near Nicolet, QC. Tragically, 8 children were killed in the accident. As a result, there were updates to 'Le Code de la securité routière' regarding the transportation of children.

On March 16th, the "Patrician", a fishing schooner from Shelburne, NS, attempted to take shelter from a storm and collided with Black Rock Ledges near Gull Rock, NS. All 10 individuals aboard perished.

On March 18th at 1:27pm (local), a fire broke out at A. Hollander & Sons fur dyers in Montreal, QC. Soon after, an explosion collapsed part of the building. As a result, 5 individuals were killed and another 60 were injured.
On March 18th, a United States Air Force RB-36 encountered engine trouble and crashed on Random Island, NL. All 23 individuals on-board including an Air Force general were killed in the crash.

On March 21st, a slow-moving winter storm impacted Edmonton and its surrounding area. The winter storm had heavy snow (25 cm in west Edmonton and Stoney Plain, and over 40 cm in Westlock), blowing snow with wind gusts up to 50 km/hr, and whiteout conditions. On Highway 2 near Leduc, the RCMP closed a 60 kilometre stretch of highway after a 100 car pileup. Buses were brought in and used as temporary shelters and triage centres. There were over 100 injuries, and the clean-up took 3 days. In a collision near Westlock, 3 people were killed.

On July 17th, one of the longest storm tracts in Ontario's history left a 400 kilometre long trail of damage. The series of severe storms produced funnel clouds, straight-line winds, and tornadoes. The areas with the most significant wind damage were Larder Lake, Manitoulin Island, Verner, Sturgeon Falls, North Bay, Calendar, French River, Mattawa, and Peterborough which experienced straight-line winds between 120-170 km/hr. In the evening, 2 tornadoes (an EF 1 and an EF 0) touched down in the Newmarket area. In addition to the property damage, there was extensive damage to Hydro One infrastructure including downed high-voltage circuits, 1,000 snapped electricity poles,  4,000 damaged insulators, and over 200 damaged transformer . The storm system eventually crossed over into Quebec where it  continued to cause damage. Successive storms throughout July, August and September caused over $100 million in losses and Hydro One earned the Edison Electric Institute's Emergency Recovery Award for its outstanding efforts in restoring service.
On March 24th, the steamship "Sechelt" sank near Race Rocks (Sooke, BC). It is reported that all 20 crew and passengers were lost.

On March 9th at 10:00pm (local), an arsonist started a series of fires including one behind the Radford-Wright building in Winnipeg, MB. Unbeknownst to the firefighters, were 2 containers of naptha - a flammable liquid - from the factory workshop within the building. When the containers exploded, the factory walls and other debris were blown outwards. The explosion killed 2 firefighters and 5 onlookers; 13 others were sent to hospital. Some reports note that 3 later died in hospital. The arsonist was eventually apprehended and confessed to starting over 200 fires.

On May 15th, a small grass fire quickly grew out-of-control and burned the community of Hebertville-Station, QC; the second time since 1930. The fire destroyed 26 buildings and damaged a further 20 buildings which left 42 families (about 275 individuals) homeless.

On May 18th, just before Victoria Day weekend, a coffee vending machine at Laval University was laced with arsenic. Within a week, 20 to 35 students and staff complained about vomiting, diarrhea, blurred vision and numbness in their limbs - symptoms of arsenic poisoning.

On May 19th, a wildfire had just been spotted when it reached and burned the small community of Lac La Biche, AB. It was an ideal fire season for the area; the winter of 1919 had a low snowfall, followed by an early spring drought, and hot and dry conditions in May. Within hours, the entire community had burned  down, except for the local inn, church, train station and a few other buildings. Property damage and inventory losses were estimated to be over $200,000 (1919 CAD). This fire, however, was part of a larger complex that stretched to Prince Albert, SK, and Meadow Lake, SK (over 300 km east). In total, the fire burned over 2 million ha (20,000 km2) of forest. Indigenous lands and people were also deeply affected by this fire. For example, the fire reached a small Cree hunting party on Sekip Lake, SK, resulting in the death of 11 individuals, and the injury of 12 others.

On May 20th, a fire broke out at the Cote Brothers show factory in Saint-Hyacinthe, QC. The hot, dry and breezy weather quickly spread the fire to nearby buildings. Within 5 hours, the fire had destroyed 29 blocks and along with it, 250 homes, and at least 9 businesses. It is estimated that the fire left a quarter of the population homeless and caused $400,000 (1903 CAD) in losses.

On May 20th, it was announced that a single breeder cow in northern Alberta tested positive for bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE). Within hours, countries that imported Canadian beef imposed trade bans. From May 2003 to May 2005, it is estimated that the Canadian beef sector lost over $2.5 billion.

In mid-April of 2007 after the seal hunt, an ice pack off northeastern Newfoundland and southern Labrador tightened and trapped over 100 fishing and sealing vessels. While some fishers were rescued, roughly 500 were stranded for up to 3 weeks.

On May 23rd, a fire broke near Rowden's Hardware store in Cobalt, ON. The fire quickly spread and over 100 volunteer firefighters from surrounding communities helped in the fire suppression efforts. In the end, the fire destroyed 140 buildings and left 459 individuals homeless. The estimated losses were $4 million (1977 CAD). Many residents did not rebuild in Cobalt; between the 1971 and 1981 Census, the population of Cobalt dropped by almost 20%.

On May 28th, heavy rains caused the Paquette electricity Dam along the Current River in Ontario to fail. Roughly 200 million cubic feet of water was released down river and into Port Arthur, ON. As a result, the floodwaters destroyed kilometres of Canadian Pacific Railway tracks, caused other property and infrastructure damage, and derailed a freight train. The dam failure killed 5 individuals, all of whom were on the freight train, and caused an estimated $500,000 (1908 CAD) in losses.

On May 5th, the American fishing schooner "Gloriana" ran ashore at Thrum Cape, near Canso, NS. During the initial collision, 3 individuals were able to climb the cliff that the schooner had collided with. But the waves soon brought the schooner out-of-reach and the remaining 15 fisherman and sailors perished.

On May 7th, the passenger ship "RMS Lusitania" was returning to Liverpool after departing from New York when it was torpedoed by a German U-Boat off the coast of Ireland. The ship was carrying 1,960 passengers and crew as well as war supplies. The ship sank in 18 minutes killed 1,198 individuals. While it is difficult to ascertain the number of Canadians who perished in the sinking, as Canadians were listed as British during this period, it is estimated that dozens of Canadian were killed.

On November 11th, residents of Leduc, AB, were returning from a Remembrance Day ceremony to meet at the local hotel between noon to 2:00pm. A few minutes before noon (local), there was an explosion that weakened the walls causing the collapse of the first storey. Soon after, a second explosion occurred, this time with a fire. The powerful explosion could be heard over 27 km away. Both explosions were caused from gas seeping into the Leduc Hotel basement. As a result, 10 people were killed and 16 were injured.

On November 14th, a nor'easter moved into the Great Lakes region and impacted Lake Erie, Lake St. Clair and Lake Huron in particular. In 1972, Lake Erie was already at record high levels. During the storm, water gages registered a 2.4 m (8 ft) difference in water level between Buffalo, NY and Toledo, Ohio. This event led to significant property damage along the shoreline; an estimated $22 million (USD 1973).

On November 15th, over 150 mm of rain fell on Vancouver in 15 hours. By noon, 7 provincial highways were blocked with eight communities experiencing power outages. Additionally, several landslides in Vancouver water reservoirs created a risk of water contamination resulting in a boil water advisory for 2 million residents in Vancouver and its surrounding area. While the advisory was partially lifted the next day, almost a million residents in Vancouver, Burnaby, and the North Shore remained under a boil water advisory for 10 more days. This was the largest water warning in Canadian history. This storm and a series of storms over the next month would lead to over $133 million (CAD 2006) in insured losses.

On November 19th at 4:16pm (local), 2 GO trains collided in Toronto. One train was carrying over 800 passengers and had just departed Union Station. The second train was empty, and was reversing on the same line as the first. Although this was a relatively low speed collision (the first train at ~20 km/hr and the second at ~3 km/hr), 54 passengers and 2 crew members sustained minor injuries.

On November 19th, a winter storm caused a series of accidents that blocked a section of the TransCanada highway near Cobequid Pass along the Nova Scotia and New Brunswick border. Over 1,500 vehicles were stranded for 14 hours overnight along a 12 kilometre stretch of highway.

On November 20th at 6:20pm (local), a VIA rail passenger train struck a piece of rail that was intentionally placed on the track causing a fire that engulfed part of the locomotive and 2 passenger cars. The fire started almost immediately; windows began to shatter and melt as flames and smoke filled the first passenger car. When the passengers could not open the door to the next car, individuals began to panic - smashing out car windows and jumping from the train while still moving. When the door between the cars was opened, the second passenger car was in the same predicament. Eventually all passengers and on-board service employees were able to exit the 2 engulfed cars and locomotives. The other passenger cars were minimally affected and successfully evacuated. Of the 385 passengers, 15 were seriously injured and 31 had minor injuries.

On November 23rd, the Steamer "Sylvanus J. Macy" was carrying coal from Buffalo, NY, en route to Wisconsin when it encountered strong gales (wind) on Lake Erie. The Steamer was last seen by the barge "Mabel Wilson" off Port Burwell, ON, before it foundered. All 18 individuals on-board perished.

On November 27th, a windstorm resulted in serious impacts across the Calgary area, including impeding traffic in the downtown core. The windstorm caused over $172 million in insured losses (CAD 2011).

On October 10th, the Steamer "City of Monticello", a steamer with the Saint John, NB, to Yarmouth, NS, route, foundered in a storm near the Yarmouth lighthouse. There were only few survivors, and 36 crew and passengers perished.
On October 17th, a Queen Charlotte Airlines flight from Kitimat, BC, to Vancouver crashed into Mount Benson in poor weather conditions. All 23 individuals on board were killed.

On October 20th, 1916 - also known as Black Friday - high winds and waves blowing across Lake Erie foundered 4 ships. The whaleback freighter the James B. Colgate left Buffalo harbour just after midnight en route to Fort William (now Thunder Bay). By 8:00pm (local) that evening, the crashing waves  as well as a shift in the coal caused the "James B. Colgate" to list; it sank 2 hours later off Erieau, ON. Of the crew of 26, only Captain Grashaw survived. He was adrift for 35 hours before being rescued by the "Marquette & Bessemer No. 2 II". The Black Friday storm also foundered a schooner - the "D.L. Filer" (killing 6 of its 7 crew); a lumber hooker - the "Marshall F. Butters" (all 13 survived); and a Canadian steamer - the "Merida" (killing all 23 abroad). On these 4 ships, 54 individuals perished.

On October 23rd, the "SS Regulus" was damaged in bad weather and tugs from Petty Harbour, NL, went to assist. At 10:00pm (local), the SS Regulus was found but the attempt to tow the steamer failed. Roughly 2 hours later, the SS Regulus ran aground at Shoal Bay, and all 19 individuals aboard were lost.

Between July 3rd and 9th, a heat wave gripped Ontario and Quebec. In Toronto, paramedics received 51% more complaints about breathing problems and 39% more calls related to fainting. In Ottawa, the RCMP musical ride was cancelled. In Montreal, heat-related deaths doubled. Across 8 health regions of Quebec, there was a 33% increase in mortality rate (280 excess deaths).
On October 31th, an explosion at Brazeau Collieries Ltd west of Rocky Mountain House, AB, killed 29 miners.

On October 3rd at around 7:00pm (local), after making a scheduled stop in Botwood, NL, an American Export Airlines from New York, NY, to Ireland crashed on take-off. Of the 37 individuals on board, 26 survived and 11 were killed.

On October 7th at 7:35pm (local), a school bus was struck by a freight train at a train crossing in Dorion, QC. The bus was carrying over 40 students going to a nearby school dance. The bus had stopped at lowered gates at the rail crossing for a passenger trail, as the gates lifted the school bus proceeded across the tracks only to be struck by a 101-car freight train. Tragically, 18 students and the bus driver were killed almost instantly, two students later died from their injuries sustained in the crash.

On October 8th, a logging truck collided with a family hayride in the small community of Cormier Village, NB. The truck tipped as it was passing the hayride and tonnes of logs came down on the riders. The hayride was part of a large family reunion on the Thanksgiving weekend. In total, 13 individuals were killed and a further 45 were injured.
On September 10th, the cable of a mine cage carrying 16 miners at the Extension Mine near Nanaimo, BC, broke. The cage and the miners dropped roughly 90 m (300 ft.); there were no survivors.

On September 18th, an international flight from Brussels, Belgium, to New York, NY, crashed roughly 35 km south west of Gander, NL. The aircraft was scheduled to stop in Gander on its way to New York, but crashed in bad weather. Of the 7 crew members and 37 passengers on board, the crash claimed 27 lives. There were 17 survivors (1 crew member and 16 passengers).

On September 18th, at 8:32am (local) during the morning rush hour in Ottawa, a VIA rail passenger train struck an OC Transpo (city transit) double decker bus at a crossing. As a result of the collision, the front of the bus was sheared off and the train was derailed. On the bus, there were 9 fatalities, 9 serious injuries, and roughly 25 minor injuries.

On September 21st, the Midland Foundry & Machine Company were celebrating a special event aboard the Wawinet yacht when it suddenly listed and sank near Beausoleil Island in Georgian Bay. Of the 42 aboard, 25 perished.
On September 23rd, a fire broke out in the kitchen of the Cecil Hotel in Dawson City, YT, which burned down a large portion of the community's business district.

At the end of 1987, precipitation amounts were below normal across western Canada. The winter season also had below average snow accumulation. The drought in 1988 extended across North America which was compounded by high temperatures and low relative humidity. Agricultural production and crop yields were significantly impacted in southern Alberta and southern Manitoba, however, it was exceptionally severe in southern Saskatchewan. For example, agricultural production in Saskatchewan was roughly 49% of the 10-year average. Of the 325 farms that went bankrupt in Canada in 1988, 115 of those were in Saskatchewan. The estimated losses were $4.1 billion (in 2000 dollars).
On September 2nd, an Airwest Airlines from Victoria, BC, crashed on approach to the Vancouver Harbour water aerodrome. Of the 13 individuals on board, 11 were killed.

On September 3rd at 1:50am (local), a VIA rail passenger train derailed near Biggar, SK. Of the 2 locomotives and 19 cars, all but 6 derailed. Because of the time of day, most of the passengers and on-train service employees were asleep. Of the 198 individuals on board, 1 was fatally injured, 13 were seriously injured and 65 had minor injuries.
On the afternoon of December 9th, an explosion at the Galt No. 8 mine near Coalhurst, AB, killed 16 miners; at least 3 others were seriously injured.

On the afternoon of February 26th, a fire broke out at Hochelaga Protestant school in Montreal, QC. The fire began in the basement and quickly spread. At the time, there were roughly 150 students in 4 classrooms. Residents and firefighters climbed ladders to save children being handed out of the windows by teachers. Sadly, not all could be saved; 16 children between the ages of 3 and 8 were killed alongside the young principal of the school. She made an extraordinary effort to save as many children as she could, and as a result, the school was rebuilt in her memory: Sarah Maxwell Memorial School.

On the evening of August 14th, the "SS Islander", a steamer owned by the Canadian Pacific Steam Navigation Company, left Skagway, Alaska, en route to Vancouver. Within 8 hours, the steamer had struck an iceberg and foundered. While there were several survivors, between 40 and 65 individuals perished.

On the evening of May 15th, an unidentified plane showed up on radar near Ottawa and two CF-100 interceptors (military jets) were dispatched from RCAF Uplands. After it was determined that the unidentified plane was a RCAF transport plane that had arrived ahead of schedule, the two aircrafts began their return to the air base. At 10:37pm (local), one of the military jets crashed into the chapel at the Villa-Louis Convent run by the Grey Nun's of the Cross in Orleans, ON. The impact ignited the jet fuel and munitions on board causing an explosion. In total, 15 individuals were killed including; 13 civilians and the 2 crew members. The cause of the crash was never determined.

On the evening of October 13th, the passenger ferry "Caribou" crossing the Cabot Strait between North Sydney, NS, and Port aux Basque, NL, began its journey. On board were 73 civilians (11 children), 118 military personnel, and 46 crew. At 3:40 am (local) on October 14th, the SS Caribou was torpedoed by a German U-boat and sank. Of the 237 aboard, 136 perished including 57 military personnel, 49 civilians and 10 of the 11 children.

On the evening of October 26th, Victoria experienced its second "Great Fire"; only 3 years after the first. The fire began in Spencer's Department store (Spencer's Arcade) and spread to the nearby buildings in the Five Sisters Block. The damage to Spencer's Arcade was $600,000 (~1910 CAD).

On the evening of October 30th, an American Airlines flight from New York, NY, to Chicago, IL, crashed on a farm near Lawrence Station, ON. Of the 20 crew members and passengers on board, there were no survivors.

On the evening of September 14th, the steamer "Manasoo" left Manitoulin Island for Owen Sound, ON, with 116 head of cattle. As the Manasoo sailed from Lake Huron to Georgian Bay, the winds picked up which caused the steamer to pitch, and then list. In the early hours of the 15th, the Manasoo rolled near Griffith Island. Only 6 crew members managed to find a lifeboat and drifted for 3 days; one man died a few hours before being rescued. In the end, 16 crew members perished.

On the evening of September 19th, a fire broke out in the basement of the Beauval Residential school in Beauval, SK. The fire quickly spread up two stairways and quickly trapped those in the boys' dormitory. Tragically, 19 children, all boys aged 7 to 12, and 1 nun perished in the fire.

On the morning of April 27th, a submarine landslide on the Kitimat River delta at low tide created a tsunami in Kitimat Arm, BC. The tsunami moved from Moon Bay, struck the wharf and terminal facilities at Kitimat, and then moved across the inlet to Kitamaat Village - Haisla Nation. The tsunami moved down the bay affecting other inlets. The wave had a peak height of 8.2 m, was associated with a rapid withdrawal of water, and lasted about an hour. Damage to the shore installations and buildings was $600,000.

On the morning of December 7th, the "Marquette & Bessemer No. 2" train car ferry left Conneaut, Ohio, en route to Port Stanley, ON. The Marquette & Bessemer No. 2 was carrying 30 rail cars, a crew of about 30 and a passenger. By the afternoon, the temperature dropped below 0°C and the winds were 120 km/hr;  many ice-covered ships returned to port. A lifeboat carrying nine crew members was found adrift 24 km from Erie, Pennsylvania, all crew members succumbed to the elements. The wreckage of the Marquette & Bessemer No. 2 is thought to be located off Long Point, ON.

On the morning of July 31st, a Colonial Coach Lines bus travelling from Toronto to Montreal struck a stalled transport truck along Highway 2 near Morrisburg, ON, and fell into the Williamsburg canal. Several passengers were able to escape through broken windows, however, 20 were killed in the accident.

On the morning of June 23rd, Canada's largest onshore earthquake occurred - a M7.5 earthquake (MM VIII) near the Forbidden Plateau area of Vancouver Island. This earthquake was felt as far as Portland, Oregon, Prince Rupert, BC, and in the Rocky Mountains. Nearby communities such as Courtenay, Campbell River, Cumberland and Union Bay experienced considerable damage; 75% of chimneys were thrown down in some communities.  Chimney damage was noted as far as Victoria. A chimney collapse at an elementary school in Courtenay fell into the building, through the roof and onto the desks of a classroom below - luckily the earthquake occurred outside of school hours. The earthquake also caused soil failure, landslides and a landslide-generated displacement wave (tsunami). The tsunami affected parts of the Georgia Strait and nearby inlets; the maximum wave height was 2 m. Of the 2 deaths reported, one was a heart attack in Seattle, the other was a drowning when a boat capsized in the displacement wave near Mapleguard Point.

On the morning of September 12th, a fire broke out at Roller Mills - a local plaster and grist mill in Paris, ON, and quickly spread and burned over half of Paris' downtown area including over 20 businesses. The high winds were due to the remnants of the Great Galveston Hurricane system that was crossing southern Ontario at the time. The damage is estimated to be $200,000 (1900 CAD).
