Within 40 minutes, the surface fire reached the edge of the community, and within the day, the wildfire moved quickly through the village. The wildfire destroyed a total of 151 buildings (out of 179 primary structures). Of these, 112 homes and businesses were in the Village of Lytton, 34 homes were in Klickkumcheen and 5 homes were in Klahkamich. As a result of the fire, two individuals perished and 1,200 were evacuated. The Lytton Creek wildfire caused an estimated $102 million in insured losses. The Lytton Creek complex comprised of the Lytton Creek, George Road, McKay Creek, and Mowhokam Creek fires. This fire complex burned a total of 836.7km2 (83,671 ha) and was classified as "under control" on September 5th.

In 2021, Northern Ontario experienced an exceptional fire season - northwestern Ontario was particularly affected. Between April 1st and October 31st, 1,198 fires were recorded which burned 7,933 km2 (793,325 ha); this was above the 10-year average. Ideal fire conditions were perpetuated by a drought which was centered over southern Manitoba and eventually creeped into northwestern Ontario in the spring. The hot and dry conditions peaked in the summer with extreme and exceptional drought. The Province of Ontario requested federal assistance and the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) were deployed on July 12th. CAF members supported local response and evacuation efforts in remote communities. Support was continued until September 12th.

Throughout the fall of 2020 and into the winter and spring of the next year, Manitoba received very little precipitation. On March 22nd, the first wildfire was reported which was much earlier than in previous seasons. The wildfires were above the 20 year average and 12,600 km2 (1.26 million ha) were burned. The province requested federal assistance on July 20th and roughly 100 Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) members and resources were mobilized to aid in suppression efforts. While overall impacts were low in the province, the most significant fire(s) where those that destroyed hydro line infrastructure to remote communities. In July, the loss of hydro lines delivering power to Little Grand Rapids First Nation and Pauingassi led to an extended evacuation of 1,553 residents until October. Wildfires damaged approximately 100 poles; many of these were "rock sets" which required specialized equipment to re-install.

place: Regional District of the Central Okanagan, BC
comment: On July 13th, a wildfire was spotted 10 km west of Vernon. On August 5th, after jumping the highway, the wildfire burned the community of Monte Lake. The White Rock Lake wildfire Fire (K61884) burned a total of 833 km2 (83,342 ha) and affected the regions of Killiney Beach, the Salmon River watershed, Monte Lake and as far as Okanagan Lake. As a result of the fire, 85 structures were destroyed; 10 homes and 1 business in the Okanagan Indian Band (Reserve No.1); 75 properties in the Regional District of the Central Okangan as well as some in the Regional District of North Okanagan and on Crown land. The White Rock Lake wildfire caused an estimated $77 million in insured losses.

On October 4th, the City of Iqaluit began responding to reports of a fuel odour in the drinking water. After continued testing, Iqaluit recommended a boil water advisory on October 12th with water being delivered by truck. A few days later, the city reported a high concentration of fuel contaminants in an in-ground water tank. The cause of the petroleum hydrocarbon contamination was from a historical below-ground fuel storage tank buried adjacent to the water treatment plant. On October 20th, Iqaluit declared a State of Emergency. Two days later, the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) were requested to help in the efforts including the use of two Reverse Osmosis Water Purification Units and operators. The old fuel tank was removed on November 19th. On December 10th, the Nunavut Chief Public Health Officer lifted the "do not consume" order and the state of emergency continued until December 14.

In 2021, Southern British Columbia experienced a wetter-than-normal fall. In many places, September and October were already twice as wet as normal. On November 13th, a significant weather system (atmospheric river) tracked across southern Vancouver Island to the Fraser Valley. For 2.5 days, a substantial amount of rain fell; in some places it was between 200-300mm. For example, in Agassiz, BC, 232.5 mm of rain fell between November 13th and 16th. An already saturated ground meant that most of the water pooled, overtopped river banks and/or flowed over the surface. As a result, there was widespread and significant flooding across much of southern BC and Vancouver Island. Mudslides and fast-moving water trapped motorists on major highways. For example, 300 individuals, 26 dogs and 1 cat required evacuation via helicopter on Highway 7. Significantly damaged and/or washed out transportation routes caused months of closures. Several communities also flooded. One of the largest communities that was impacted was Merritt in which its entire population of 7,000 residents was evacuated. Another significantly impacted region was the Sumas Prairie area of Abbotsford where over 1,000 homes were flooded and 1,000s of farm animals perished. The community of Princeton was also significantly affected. At one point, the combination of flooding, landslides, washouts and bridge collapses led to Vancouver being disconnected from the rest of southwestern BC by road, pipeline and rail. A provincial State of Emergency was declared on November 17th, and the members of the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) were deployed to aid in the efforts which included delivering food/supplies, sandbagging, constructing dams, evacuating 30,000 chickens, among other tasks. The CAF operation ended on December 17th. On November 19th, the Province of British Columbia requested financial assistance from the federal government. However, cascading impacts continued and ranged from severed supply chains from transportation network disruptions to agricultural losses to exports/import delays. Insured losses were estimated to be $687 million (CAD 2021). It is estimated that 1.3 million animals including at least 640,000 farm animals perished in the floodwaters. As a result, the Province has undertaken several flood recovery projects including one for highways in which Highways 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 11, 19 and 99, among others, will address the transportation impact. In many locations and sectors, it is estimated that it will take years to recover from this event. This was not the only rain event BC experienced in November of 2021; three more atmospheric rivers tracked over the area in the weeks following.

In late November, a multi-day storm tracked over Atlantic Canada which brought significant rain and wind. Ingonish Beach on Cape Breton, for example, recorded 232.8 mm of rain on November 23rd alone. In Port aux Basques, NL, 165.1 mm of rain fell between November 23-24th and had accompanying winds of 96 km/hr. The rain caused extreme flooding that washed out transportation infrastructure not only throughout southwestern Newfoundland, but also on Cape Breton Island and other regions of Atlantic Canada. In addition to many residents being stranded and displaced, the road washouts in Newfoundland hindered service and product deliveries to the rest of the province because of the washouts near Port aux Basques. From November 25th to December 2nd, the Canadian Armed Forces were deployed to assist in the efforts including transporting 70 individuals and 1,550 pounds of cargo into and out of the affected area(s). On December 21st and February 24th 2022, the Provinces of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador, respectively, requested financial assistance from the federal government.

In mid-January, an Alberta Clipper tracked across western Canada. Widespread power outages were reported in BC where 220,000 customers on Vancouver Island, the Gulf Islands, the Lower Mainland and the Southern Interior were without power on January 13th. This system and its high winds continued to track through Alberta and into Saskatchewan. Throughout January 13th in Saskatchewan, rain changed over to snow and blowing snow causing blizzard-like conditions. It was the significant sustained wind and wind gusts, however, that caused most of the damage. In Bratt's Lake - just south of Regina - wind gusts of 135 and 142 km/hr were reported on January 13th and 14th, respectively. This winter storm impacted four provinces causing a total of $134 million in insured losses with most of the losses being recorded in Saskatchewan.

On July 2nd, ideal conditions for severe thunderstorm development existed across the foothills and Calgary region. These storms tracked over Calgary in the mid-afternoon and continued for another 5-6 hours. This brought significant localized rain (25-50 mm) which led to pluvial/urban flooding and basement sewer backups. In a span of two hours, Emergency Services responded to 200 calls. However, it was the hail that caused the most damage. As a result, there were 39,000 insurance claims totalling over $570 million (CAD 2021) in insured losses; 16,000 claims ($128 million) were for vehicles damage alone.

At 2:30pm (local) on July 15th, an EF2 tornado tracked over the neighbourhoods of Painswick and Bayshore estates in Barrie, ON, south of Kempenfelt Bay. The 510 m wide tornado reached a wind speed of up to 210 km/hr and travelled a total of 12.5 km. Both neighbourhoods experienced significant damage and over 2,200 insurance claims were filed. Of the 150 damaged homes, 71 were left uninhabitable. Furthermore, 700 vehicles were also damaged. As a result of this EF2 tornado, 11 individuals were injured and there was $107 million in insured losses. This weather system produced a total of 10 tornadoes throughout central Ontario from the Lake Simcoe area through to Algonquin Park and north of Pembroke.

On December 11th, a system moved through southern Ontario and into Quebec producing winds over 100 km/hr. In Port Colborne, for example, winds were recorded at 130 km/hr. As a result, there were widespread power outages and wind damage. Hydro One reported that by the end of December 11 over 535,000 customers were affected. The extensive power outages were partly due to the number of trees that fell onto power lines in addition to 250 broken polls. Hydro-Quebec reported that upwards of 400,000 customers lost power. The windstorm caused an estimated $152 million in insured losses; with over $100 million being incurred in Ontario, $40 million in Quebec and just under $10 million in the Atlantic provinces.
provinces: ON QC NS PE NL NB

comment: In the last 1.5 weeks of June, an exceptionally large and stable high pressure system moved over western North America. The pressure system, combined with persistent drought and the solar altitude (longest days of the year) created a significant heat event for roughly 11 days. Both Canada and the United States experienced temperatures that were 15-25C above average. The Canadian heat record was broken three times on three consecutive days in Lytton, BC. On June 27th, heat record was broken when Lytton reached 45.2C (former was on July 5, 1937 in Yellow Grass and Midale SK at 45C). The next day, it reached 46.3C, and June 29th was 48.6C. However, several communities broke heat records in southwestern BC; many experienced temperatures above 40C for nearly a week. In Kamloops, for example, the 84-year old record was broken. This heat event caused power outages, damaged paved surfaces (from buckling to melting), and led to crop losses, in addition to compounding wildfire conditions. This heat wave was the 'hottest week in Canadian history'. As a result, there were 569 heat-related deaths in British Columbia and a further 185 in Alberta; 650,000 farm animals and over a billion marine mammals were also estimated to have also perished from the heat.
provinces: AB BC MB NB NL NT NS NU ON PE QC SK YT

comment: On July 5th, a tornado moved through the communities of Carievale and Gainsborough, SK, and the storm continued to track through to Pierson, MB. Several homes and farms were destroyed. As a result, 5 were killed in the Gainsborough area and another 50 individuals were injured.

At 3:58 am (local) on March 20th, two trains collided along the CN railway at Mileage 44 (Drocourt) roughly 55 km north of Parry Sound, ON. Train No. 3 was en route to Winnipeg, while train No. 4 was en route to Toronto when they collided head-on. The most fatalities occurred when a passenger car telescoped into the baggage car of train No. 3. and subsequently caught fire. It is estimated that 19 individuals perished in the rail accident, although the final number will never be known. Many of those who perished were immigrants who were settling in the West; most had no family connections in Canada.

At 7:30am (local) on September 12th, an eastbound train collided with another along the CPR railway in Azilda, ON (just west of Sudbury). The'Harvesters Special' was a passenger train full of seasonal workers from the east going to help with the annual harvests in the Prairies. The train had stopped and was ready to pull onto a siding when the accident occurred. The second train (No 2. 'Imperial Limited') was running late and attempted to stop, but the rear brakes of the train failed. Train No 2 was unable to stop and collided with the 'Harvesters Special' sending the baggage car into a passenger car. As a result, 12 were killed and another 24 were injured.

On the morning of November 10th, an inter-urban rail link (streetcar 'Sumas') between Vancouver and New Westminster was struck by falling timbers from a flat car. The flat car was loaded with timbers when it uncoupled from the rest of the train and rolled downhill along the track. The force of the movement was enough to release the timbers where they were thrown into the 'Sumas'. At the time, the 'Sumas' was carrying commuters on their way to work (who  most worked for the BC Electric Railway). Of the 24 passengers, 15 were killed and another 8 were seriously injured.

July 7th was a warm summer's day and ideal for picnicking. Hundreds (including two Sunday School groups from Toronto) flocked to the parks of Queenston and Niagara Falls to enjoy the weather. At 7:15pm (local), however, it began to rain and many boarded the electric trains (trolley) back to Niagara Falls and Toronto. Typical coaches carried 60-80 people, but on the evening of July 7th, it was estimated that 160 had piled on-board. As the train travelled down the escarpment at Queenston Heights, a series of technical failures occurred. First, the train slipped off the overhead wire depriving the driver of some driving capabilities including the reverse gear, then both the air brakes and emergency brakes failed thus leaving the packed train/trolley without any control as it went down the escarpment. On the third turn, it jumped the tracked and plunged down an embankment. As a result, 15 were killed and at least 92 were injured.

Between January 9th and 11th, roughly 25.3 cm of snow fell in Brandon, MB. On January 12th, the maximum temperature reached was -36.1C creating ideal conditions for ice fog. That morning, a CP rail snow crew was busy clearing the tracks in the railyard and took a short break in a caboose car. Soon thereafter, a freight train leaving the yards struck the other train. In the low visibility and even travelling at a low speed was still enough to send to empty flatcars into the caboose. As a result, 19 workers were killed.

At 7:14am (local) on December 20th, a passenger train collided with a freight train roughly 3.7 km west of Onawa, Maine, along the Canadian Pacific Railway (CPR). The westbound passenger train was travelling between St John, NB, and Montreal, QC, and was carrying passengers from the steamship 'Empress of France'. The eastbound train was carrying freight. The force of the collision interlocked the engines. The baggage car of the passenger train also crumpled into the engines and two passenger cars were telescoped and caught fire. As a result, 19 passengers and 4 employees were killed and a further 68 others were injured. The passenger train was carrying mostly English and Scottish immigrants who had just landed in Canada as well as some Canadian soldiers.

At midnight (local) on March 21st, a major fire began at a downtown restaurant in Nicolet, QC. The fire was quickly spread by strong winds and destroyed 35 buildings in the downtown area including shops, banks, offices, restaurants and homes. The fire was brought under control by 6:00am. As a result, 75 households (300 individuals) were left homeless, however, there were no reported deaths or serious injuries. The fire was estimated to have caused almost $1 million in losses (CAD 1955).

In the first two weeks of July, a heat wave gripped eastern North America including Canada. For example, temperatures in Toronto exceeded 35C for six consecutive days; the highest being 39.4C on July 3rd. It was reported that at least 58 deaths occurred due to excessive heat in Toronto alone.

In mid to late July, ideal fire conditions (e.g. high temperatures) existed across northeastern Ontario. At the time, it was common practice to use fire to clear land. On July 29th, a wildfire burned near Cochrane, ON, and moved into the business district and part of the residential section of the community. Many residents fled by rail or into the nearby lake to take refuge from the fire. In order to keep communications between communities, Miss E Jameson stayed at her station and kept the telephone lines open as long as possible. The townships of Glackmeyer, Kennedy and Lamarche were also deeply affected by the wildfire. A total of 230 properties in Cochrane alone were destroyed. At least 20 individuals were killed, and numerous were injured. Although separate fires, the Great Matheson fire occurred at the same time.

On May 18th, a fire caused a dynamite explosion in the magazine in Cobalt, ON. The fire quickly spread and burned 65 homes. Many residents and miners aided in the fire suppression effort and managed to put out the fire before more of the community was burned.

At 11:00pm (local) on August 20th, a local physician put out a small yet suspicious fire behind a building in the downtown area of Haileybury, ON. Only a few hours later, at 3:00am, another fire began behind a local shop. Within five hours, the business section was destroyed. It was reported that 8 blocks with 66 businesses and 10 dwellings had burned. Dynamite was used to create firebreaks which was credited for saving the northern part of the community.As a result, many businesses had to operate out of tents until buildings were rebuilt.The fire caused an estimated $150,000 (CAD 1911) in losses. Given the suspicious circumstances, this fire was investigated by the Provincial Inspector.

Following a devastating fire in the same month, a typhoid epidemic swept through the community of Cobalt, ON. The first few cases of typhoid appeared in early July, however, these were largely ignored by the authorities and went unreported. Finally in August, the Council requested assistance from the provincial Board of Health; although the Council refused help from nearby communities. On September 8th, the Provincial Medical Inspector and three other health inspectors arrived in Cobalt and took over, but there was little support. It wasn’t until the possibility of the entire community being quarantined that the local health board helped. Within days, over 550 clean-up notices were given, but only few complied. Fifty individuals were fined including two municipal councillors and the chairperson of the local board of health. By the end of October, the provincial inspectors removed over 1,200 wagon loads of waste and 74 polluted wells were filled. There were 1,100 cases of typhoid and 73 related deaths. The community only had one hospital that was operated by the Temiskaming Mine Managers' Association and military tents needed to be erected to house the extra patients.

On the evening of November 13th, the schooner 'Amoria' carrying 11 passengers hit early-setting ice on lac Pasteur, QC, and sank. As a result, 10 individuals perished including Reverend Pere Auguste Tortellier.

Around June 12th, a wildfire began near Traverse Brook, NL. Over the course of three months, the fire impacted 18 communities across the central and northern Bonavista Bay region. The most impacted communities were Hare Bay, Brookfield, and Carmanville where a total of 27 homes and several businesses were destroyed. Roughly 16 communities were evacuated by both car and boat including the Northern Ranger. The wildfire known as the "Bonavista North fire" was declared out in September. The total burned area measured 1,999 km2 (199,914 ha). The loss of valuable timber greatly hindered the industry-based communities in the area. In Hare Bay, for example, over 60 families left the community.

At 9:35pm (local) on May 23rd, the Chisholm fire was reported near a Canadian National railway line near Slave Lake, AB. The fire rapidly grew to 30 km2 (3,000 ha) by the morning. On May 25th, the wildfire threatened the community of Chisholm where it was evacuated at 11:30pm; a second evacuation took place on May 27th. With ideal conditions, the wildfire travelled 35 km between May 27th and 28th and joined with another wildfire (fire 73). By May 31st, it had burned within 10 km of Smith, Hondo and Slave Lake. The Chisholm fire destroyed 10 homes as well as 49 other outbuildings and vehicles; most of which were in the Hamlet of Chisholm. There was also notable damage to oil and gas infrastructure (nine companies were impacted) as well as railway and electrical infrastructure (203 distribution poles and 15 transmission structures). Significant fire resources were used in the fire efforts including 514 firefighters, 34 helicopters, 31 bulldozers and 84 other fire management personnel. The burned area measured 1,097 km2 (109,744 ha). In addition to the property losses, the fire burned 4.5 million m3 of growing lumber stock. Additionally, portions of the threatened woodland caribou habitat (Slave Lake herd) was extensively damaged.

In mid-January of 1963, 1,500 members of the Lumber and Sawmill Workers Union decided to strike after a contract dispute with their employer (the Spruce Falls Power and Paper Company). The mill relied on pulpwood supplied by a local woodcutters cooperative. The striking workers asked the woodcutters to stop supplying wood to the mill in order to apply further pressure on their employer - but they refused. Tensions escalated when strikers sabotaged and/or blockaded the pulpwood shipments. The conflict culminated just after midnight (local) on February 11th when 400 workers went to the train yards at Reeser Siding to halt the loading of pulpwood. Although 20 Ontario Provincial Police officers had created a chain to block the workers, they were able to breach the line and moved in closer to the wood. In an attempt to protect their wood, 20 armed woodcutters began to shoot into the crowd. As a result, 3 workers were killed and another 8 were injured. After the conflict, 200 police officers and a mediator were sent to the area, and the strike ended 7 days later.

In 2021, Saskatchewan experienced an exceptional fire season. From April to June, southern Saskatchewan experienced moderate drought which intensified over the summer to severe, and in same regions, extreme drought. These created ideal fire conditions. The 2021 fire season extended from April with fire advisories and lasted into the fall. By May 12th, two-thirds of southern Saskatchewan was under extreme fire weather indexes. Wildfire smoke and haze also affected several communities. For example, La Ronge and Regina experienced 293 and 147 hours of smoke/haze, respectively. Because the provincial fire seasons were exceptional across much of Canada, Saskatchewan did not request any inter-agency resources. In total, 9,561 km2 (956,084 ha) burned across the province. On March 16th, 2022, the Province of Saskatchewan requested financial assistance from the federal government.

On September 10th, Hurricane Larry entered Canadian waters as a Category 2 storm with winds topping 155 km/hr. The storm also produced significant wave heights of 9.8 m with a peak wave height of 20.8 m recorded off of southwestern Newfoundland. At the mouth of Placentia Bay, wave heights were 8.1m with a maximum height of 13.8m. The storm lingered offshore for a day before making landfall at around midnight (local) on September 11th. Now at a Category 1 hurricane, Larry tracked west of the Avalon Peninsula with sustained winds of 130 km/hr and gusts up to 180 km/hr. Hurricane Larry transitioned to a post-tropical storm at around noon on September 11th as it moved over Newfoundland. Because of its fast-moving pace, Larry did not produce much rainfall and is more known for its widespread windfield. The storm caused widespread power outages (61,000 customers), tree damage, and damage to coastal infrastructure. Among other things, the storm also caused significant coastal erosion from overwash, the storm surge and a pounding surf. As a result, there were over 2,220 insurance claims that totalled over $25 million (CAD 2021) in insured losses in Newfoundland. On October 8th, the Province of Newfoundland and Labrador requested financial assistance from the federal government.

In 2021, British Columbia experienced an exceptional fire season. In the months leading up to the season, southern BC experienced below-average precipitation with only 30% of their normal June rainfall. Extreme wildfire conditions peaked in the same month and persisted into July. In the first two weeks of July, roughly 40 new wildfires were reported daily. Between April 1st and March 28th, 2022, 1,642 fires were recorded which burned a total of 8,693 km2 (869,279 ha). On July 21st, the Province of British Columbia declared a State of Emergency which continued for 56 days before ending on September 14th. On July 29th, the Province of British Columbia requested financial assistance from the federal government. Wildfires affected communities within each of BC's Census Divisions; the most devastating was the Lytton Creek fire complex. As a result of the fire season, there were 181 evacuation orders. The Province of British Columbia also requested federal assistance from the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) who were deployed on July 5th. CAF members supported local response, helped move personnel and equipment as well as aided with wildfire suppression efforts. Support was continued until September 5th. Over the course of the deployment, roughly 300 CAF personnel supported the effort. In total, almost 4,000 personnel were involved in the response efforts; there were also 676 airtanker missions. The Province reported that $718.8 million was spent on wildfire suppression.

In mid-January, a cold wave affected most of Canada. In Winnipeg, for example, the mean temperature was below -20C from January 14th to February 5th; including 10 days with a mean below -30C. In Whitehorse, the mean daily temperature was below -30C from January 12th to January 29th; including 11 with a mean below -40C. The prolonged cold period led to a demand in energy from British Columbia to New Brunswick and it is estimated that Canadians paid an additional $500 million (CAD 1996) in energy costs that season.
provinces: AB BC MB NB NL NT NS NU ON PE QC SK YT

comment: A strong winter system tracked through the United States and into Canada on February 17th. This storm brought wind and extensive precipitation including snow, ice pellets and freezing rain to eastern Canada. For example, 41.2 mm of precipitation was recorded at Toronto's Pearson airport between February 17th-18th, and 46.6 mm in Montreal. Halifax, on the other hand, recorded 47.4 mm on February 18th alone. Although high winds were reported across eastern Canada, Beaver Island, NS, recorded 117 km/hr gusts on the 18th. It is estimated that this winter storm cost $140 million (CAD 2022) in losses across eastern Canada.
provinces: NS NB NL PE ON QC

comment: On May 21st, a mesoscale convective complex (system of thunderstorms) tracked through an area that extended over 1,000 km from southeastern Michigan through most of southwestern, central and eastern Ontario as well as into western and southern Quebec. The severe weather system also produced four tornadoes (two EF1s near London, and two EF2s near Lake Scugog) and at least 10 downbursts across the area. The most destructive downburst occurred in the City of Ottawa where at 3:45pm (local), the system moved through the area. In a 36 km by 5 km swath in the southern areas of rural Ottawa, the maximum wind speeds were 190 km/hr (the equivalent of an EF2 tornado). There was extensive and widespread structural and tree damage across the impacted areas in both Ontario and Quebec and at least 13 communities declared states of emergencies. Between Hydro One, Hydro Quebec and Hydro Ottawa, nearly 1.5 million customers were without power (30,000 were still without power a week later). Furthermore, over 4,000 hydro poles were damaged in addition to 900 transformers that had to be replaced. Hydro Ottawa alone reported over 400 damaged hydro poles and kilometres of snapped powers lines which led to over 1,000 simultaneous power outages. In Ottawa, the damage to the hydro network was worse than both the 1998 ice storm and the 2018 tornadoes - and equivalent to 4 years of construction work and repairs. Hydro Quebec reported 554,649 customers who lost power; and 1,125 hydro poles and 400 transformers had to be replaced. This event was considered to be the deadliest derecho in Canadian history which resulted in 12 deaths and at least 12 injuries. It also led to over $1.2 billion (CAD 2022) in insured losses.

On July 18th, a storm complex tracked through the Prairie provinces. At 1:10pm (local), an EF2 tornado left a 300 m by 7.8 km long swath of damage in Cypress County, AB. Ten minutes later, a downburst caused more damage in the Redcliff area (with wind speeds measuring 145 km/hr). The system moved into Saskatchewan where it continued to cause extensive wind damage. At 8:50pm, with winds of 125 km/hr, the storm damaged several buildings near Halbrite. A downburst was also recorded in Riding Mountain National Park, MB. In addition to the wind, the storm complex also brought heavy rain and hail. Brooks and Patricia, AB, recorded 57.5 mm and 88.8 mm of rain, respectively. This storm complex caused over $100 million in insured losses across multiple provinces.

In the late afternoon of September 13th, a major weather system tracked over the Montreal Metropolitan area. The system brought thunderstorms and torrential rain. Between 5:00-7:00pm (local) in L'Assomption, for example, 44.6 mm of rain fell in that two-hour period. The deluge caused widespread urban flooding across the region - basements flooded, underpasses and tunnels were impassible, and the Metro (subway) was disrupted during the afternoon rush hour. The rain caused impacts in other regions as well. In St-Henri-de-Taillon, for example, a road washout caused one death. This rain event caused almost $166 million (CAD 2022) in insurable losses alone.

In late September, post-tropical storm Fiona brought exceptional storm surges, waves and wind, as well as heavy rain to Atlantic Canada. On September 7th, Fiona began off the coast of Africa as a tropical wave and eventually formed into a tropical storm and hurricane on September 14th and 18th, respectively. On September 23rd, the category 3 hurricane merged with a frontal system and became a powerful post-tropical cyclone. Just after 3:00am (local) the next day, Fiona made landfall near Lower Whitehead, NS, with sustained wind speeds of 165 km/hr (equivalent of a category 2 hurricane). The system slowed as it passed over Nova Scotia and tracked over Quebec's Lower North Shore, and then Newfoundland. However, the intensity was still exceptionally strong. Rainfall amounts ranged from 80-150 mm; in some locations it was 30mm/hr. Wreckhouse, NL, measured sustained winds of 122 km/hr with gusts of up to 178 km/hr. As Fiona tracked across the Atlantic provinces, it also produced a significant storm surge; in some locations the sensors stopped working. Measurements suggest that the widespread storm surge was 1-1.5m (3-5 ft) above ground level, and as high as 2m (7ft) in northern Nova Scotia, southeastern New Brunswick, and northern PEI. Fiona's storm surge and wave action caused significant coastal erosion and flooding. Between Port aux Basques and Burgeo, over 100 buildings were destroyed. On Prince Edward Island, roughly 60 roads and bridges as well as six schools were damaged. At its peak, over 500,000 customers lost power, including 415,000 in Nova Scotia and 82,000 in Prince Edward Island. Fiona was the "deepest" (i.e. lowest) pressure cyclone system on record to make landfall in Canada. As a result of Fiona, three individuals perished; two drowned in the storm surge and high waves in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, and a third died as a result of generator use in Prince Edward Island. After Requests for Federal Assistance were made on September 24 and 25, the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) deployed personnel, ships and resources to Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, and Prince Edward Island. At its peak, there were just over 1,050 personnel deployed, with 748, 160, and 150 in Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and Newfoundland, respectively. Duties ranged from safety checks to the removal of debris to help crews access areas and the power grid. CAF assistance continued until roughly the second week of October. By late September, the three provinces also made requests for Federal financial assistance. Hurricane Fiona caused over $837M (CAD 2022) in insured losses.

comment: On December 22nd, a strong and slow moving weather system tracked across the midwestern United States and reached Ontario the next morning. However, as it moved through the upper Great Lakes region, it quickly intensified (sometimes referred to as "bombogenesis"). The weather system brought severe winter storm conditions including cold temperatures, snow and wind. Throughout December 23rd, the storm dropped significant precipitation and lake effect snow. Behind the system was an Arctic front, and within 18 hours, the temperature dropped by 10-15C; this was further chilled by strong winds. For example, wind gusts in Toronto were measured at 93 and 94 km/hr on December 23rd and 24th, respectively. Point Petre in Prince Edward County recorded wind gusts of 124 km/hr, and an average wind speed of over 90 km/hr between 12:00pm on the 23rd to 5:00am on Christmas Eve. There were widespread and significant disruptions to all forms of travel in Ontario - major highways were closed including Highway 401, viaRail trains were stranded and there were numerous flight cancellations. Prince Edward County was particularly hit hard. All roads in the county were closed between December 23rd and 25th. Some motorists were caught in the snow drifts and over 100 vehicles were abandoned. On some county roads, the snow was drifting over roadway signs. Significant snow and drifting also continued along the north shore of Lake Ontario through to Kingston. Several regions declared states of emergencies including Prince Edward County, Niagara, and Chatham-Kent. Both Ontario and Quebec were significantly impacted; the storm system also affected the Maritimes. The winter storm led to roughly $180 million (CAD 2022) in insurable losses across eastern Canada.

comment: In 2022, Manitoba experienced exceptional spring flooding, however, this flood season was different than others. Over the winter, almost 150 cm of snow fell over southern Manitoba; the third-most since 1872. By May 1st, five wet weather systems tracked over the province dropping extensive rain. Winnipeg also experienced its wettest spring on record. Because of the constant weather systems and the still-frozen ground, the flooding continued for eight weeks in some regions. Furthermore, flooding was not localized but experienced across the province. Forty-five communities and nine First Nation communities declared states of local emergency. Manitoba's Department of Transportation and Infrastructure estimated that the 2022 floods cost $193.5 million (CAD 2022) in pre-emptive, response and recovery efforts to that sector alone. Several of these projects were dedicated to bridge, culvert and dam inspections, rehabilitation/stabilization and replacements. On September 12th, the Province of Manitoba requested financial assistance from the federal government.

In the summer of 2022, a persistent heat dome lingered over western Canada, especially in southern British Columbia. The average temperatures in July and August in Kelowna, for example, were 30.4C and 31.1C, respectively; the highest being 38.8C on July 28th. Between July 26 and August 3rd, the BC Coroners Service reported 16 heat-related deaths - the majority were in the Fraser and Interior Health Authority regions.

The beginning of the 2022 fire season was relatively uneventful in British Columbia. However, a persistent heat dome changed fire conditions in July and into August. The first notable wildfire was the Nohomin Creek fire (K70580) which was detected on July 14th. This wildfire burned within the Stien Valley Nlaka’pamux Heritage Park and collaborative efforts helped protect areas of ecological and cultural significance. Fifteen other fires of note began between mid-July and late August. The regions most affected by wildfires were the Thompson-Okanagan, and Kootenay regions. On October 7th, the Province of British Columbia requested financial assistance from the federal government.

On May 6th, the public was notified of the ice breakup along Hay River which soon led to an ice jam at the confluence of Hay River and Great Slave Lake. To compound the flood situation, a weather system brought over 29 mm of rain beginning on the evening on May 6th and continued into May 7th. At 1:32am (local) the 7th, the Town declared a state of local emergency and put an evacuation order in place for Vale Island. Only 30 minutes later, evacuation orders were issued for the West Channel. The evacuation expanded the next day and again on May 11th which eventually covered all of Hay River. Another push and release sequence of ice along the river on May 12th caused extensive flooding in the community. Residents were able to return home on May 15th. On July 7th, the Northwest Territories requested financial assistance from the federal government.

In early 2022, COVID-19 vaccination rules required that both Canadian and American truckers were vaccinated in order to cross the border - mandates were issued by both the United States Government and the Canadian Government. This threatened the livelihood of a small group of unvaccinated truckers. With this, several individuals in the trucking industry as well as others who supported their cause, used various platforms and networks to garner support. As identified in the Government of Canada's declaration: 'The “Freedom Convoy 2022” was a manifestation of a growing movement centered on anti-government sentiments related to the public health response to the COVID-19 pandemic.' On January 22nd, two groups of protestors left British Columbia, and on January 25, the Freedom Convoy entered Ontario. On January 28th, they arrived in Ottawa. The Freedom Convoy and its supporters filled roads with trucks of all sizes and turned parks into encampments. On the same day, there was a Request for Federal Assistance as well as an Assistance to Law Enforcement. Police officers from elsewhere in the province were deployed to Ottawa. It was expected that the protesters would leave after the first weekend, but they did not. The Convoy and their supporters stayed in downtown Ottawa for three weeks, whereupon the demonstration had evolved into an illegal/unlawful occupation. On February 6th, the City of Ottawa declared a state of emergency, which was eventually followed by the Province of Ontario declaring the same on February 11th. Significant demonstrations/blockades were also occurring elsewhere in Canada including in Coutts, AB (January 29-February 14) and at the Ambassador Bridge in Windsor (February 5-13) as well as seven other ports of entries. On February 14th, for the first time in Canadian history, the federal Emergencies Act was invoked and that the Government of Canada was 'declaring that a public order emergency exists throughout Canada that necessitates the taking of special temporary measures for dealing with the emergency'. The overall impact on the City of Ottawa and its residents was substantial including excessive noise (especially from the use of air horns) and lighting fireworks on downtown streets; excessive fumes from idling diesel engines; significant traffic and city service disruptions; numerous public safety issues, threats and violence (including false 911 calls); the targeting of some residents with symbols of hate and intolerance; acute fear and anxiety; and the significant impact on businesses and the local economy. On February 18th - after the enactment of the Emergencies Act and numerous warnings from the police - a large and coordinated police operation cleared protesters and their vehicles began; this operation concluded on the 21st. It is estimated that the protests/demonstrations led to $150-210 million in lost business revenue and wages, $7 million in city costs, and $55.5 million in policing costs.

On the evening of August 31st and into September 1st, a significant rain event affected parts of central Quebec. In Quebec City, for example, 95.3 mm of rain was recorded. The rains caused severe localized flooding and landslides. In some places, rivers rose 0.5m (2 ft) during the course of the rain storm. In St. Gregoire de Montmorency, a landslide destroyed an eight-unit apartment building; this killed four of its occupants and injured another 18 individuals. A flash flood along the Portneuf River also destroyed at least three bridges and swept away numerous homes. In Portneuf, a mother and her four children in their home were drowned. Along the same river, an undermined train trestle gave way causing a train accident; the engineer and its fireman were both killed. In total, 11 individuals in Quebec perished as a result of this rain storm.

In late November, a winter storm affected eastern Quebec and the Maritime provinces. On the Iles-de-la-Madeleine, the average sustained wind speed was 65km/hr with gusts of 107 on November 29th. The wind caused widespread power outages and over 1,500 residents were left without power and communications. As a result, the Province of Quebec made a Request for Federal Assistance on November 29th. With this, two Hercules aircrafts and 27 Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) personnel were deployed to aid in the efforts. Hydro Quebec equipment and crew were transported to the Island. The CAF also conducted reconnaissance as well as door-to-door visits. Their mission finished on December 2nd.
On July 10th, a severe storm with hail tracked over Edmonton. The hail damaged almost every metal roof and broke thousands of lights. Some large hailstones measured 8cm and weighed up to 140 grams.

In the first week of May, a 30km ice jam formed along the Yukon River. On May 9th, the United States Army sent two bombers which dropped six tons of bombs to help to move the ice jam. Five Royal Canadian Air Force bombers were on route to Dawson when the ice jam finally released. The floodwaters and ice reached the community at 7:00pm (local). Over a 3.5 hour period that night, the onrush of water and ice caused significant damage and destruction including to the power house, mining buildings, banks and the railroad. Furthermore, the water flooded the downtown area and further inundated half of the residential section of the community. After the water receded, the community was littered with debris, sewer covers, and sidewalks as well as 1.2m (4 ft) sheets of ice along the main street. At the time, it was described to be the worst flooding in its history and was an estimated 1.5 m (5 ft) above the historic 1925 flood levels.

Bell Island, NL, was an important iron-ore mining and processing centre throughout the 20th century. When the Second World War broke out, it became an integral part of Canada's military-industrial effort. With this, it also became a target for Nazi Germany. Just before noon (local) on September 5th, German U-boat (U-513) sank the 'SS Saganaga' and the 'SS Lord Strathcona' at anchor in Bell Island and Little Bell Island. Two months later in the early hours of November 2nd, German U-boats struck again. This time U-518 fired torpedoes at the 'SS Rose Castle' and the French vessel 'PLM 27' and sank both. The U-boat also fired at the 'Anna T', although the torpedo missed the vessel, it did strike the pier which caused considerable damage. As a result of the attacks, 70 individuals were killed and tons of valuable iron ore was lost.

In late December of 2018 and into January, Arctic air settled over a large part of Canada which brought extreme cold. In Toronto, for example, extreme cold weather alerts were issued for every day between (and including) December 25 and January 7. In early January, the Province of Ontario made a Request for Federal Assistance. With this, the Government of Canada made the Moss Park Armoury open as a temporary emergency warming shelter and available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week for a period of two weeks.

At 7:30pm (local) on December 30th, a fire began at McColl's grocery store in West Lorne, ON. The residents of the community attempted to contain the fire using a bucket brigade as there were no firefighting apparatus nor equipment in the community. But the fire quickly spread. At least 13 businesses were destroyed and several individuals who lived above the shops lost their homes. It was estimated that the fire caused over $20,500 (CAD 1901) in losses. The town of West Lorne required support from a nearby community to respond to and recover from the event.

The 'St. Olaf' - a 305 ton iron steamer - left Quebec City on November 18th on a return trip to Pointe aux Esquimaux. The steamer was last spotted near Sheldrake, QC, on the afternoon of November 21st while on its return route. Soon after, an early-season winter storm tracked over the area. On Anticosti Island, for example, 25.4 cm of snow was recorded on the 21st and another 20.3 cm on the 23rd. The St. Olaf was believed to have been wrecked on one of the islands of Sept-Iles, however, only debris and one body was recovered. All 26 individuals (19 crew and 7 passengers) aboard perished.

On the morning of May 7th, a passenger train collided with the caboose of a work train near Dexter, ON. On that morning, the workers were busy loading ties and had just started their breakfast in the caboose when the accident occurred. As a result, 12 workers were killed and another eight were seriously injured.

Just after 2:00pm (local) on May 13th, a fire started in the downtown area of Finch, ON. Without a waterworks system nor firefighting apparatus, the residents fought the fire using a bucket brigade. Several businesses including the bank were lost in addition to several homes. The oldest church in the district (built in 1860) was also lost in the fire.  At 10:30pm the next night, a second fire began albeit in a different section on the community. This second fire burned seven businesses and six homes. Combined, the losses were estimated to be over $100,000 (CAD 1907) where less than 25% was insured.

At 6:15pm (local) on April 17th, a fire broke out at a restaurant in Latchford, ON. The fire quickly spread and within two hours, the entire downtown area was affected. Without a waterworks system nor firefighting apparatus, fire assistance was requested from the neighbouring community of Cobalt. The Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway organized and moved a fire engine and 200 volunteers to help in the fire efforts. As a result of the fire, over 50 buildings were destroyed and left over a hundred individuals homeless. Fire losses were estimated to be between $100,000 and $150,000 (CAD 1907); most of which was not insured.

At 6:00pm (local) on June 18th, a large fire burned a few blocks in the downtown area of Pembroke, ON. The strong winds enabled the fire to spread quickly along multiple blocks. By 11:00pm, the fire was deemed under control. As a result of the fire, roughly a dozen businesses were destroyed and 30 households were left homeless.

On September 3rd, two brothers were involved in the initial planning and preparation of armed attacks on the James Smith Cree Nation, SK. The first armed attack occurred at 5:30am (local) September 4th when the brothers forcibly entered a home. After this attack, a disagreement between the brothers led to one fatally injuring the other. Over the course of the morning, the remaining brother killed 10 individuals and injured another 17 others. All but one of the fatalities occurred on the James Smith Cree Nation; the other in the neighbouring community of Weldon. The next day, the perpetrator was spotted in a stolen vehicle traveling 150 km/hr where an unmarked police vehicle forced it off the road and into a ditch. The individual was then arrested. Minutes later, the individual began to show signs of medical distress and was taken to hospital where they later died.

Following a series of avalanches that caused a train derailment at Albert Canyon, BC, rail workers were sent to clear the tracks. On March 2nd, a runaway tender (coal-car) struck and killed several of the workers before colliding with the derailed freight engine. As a result, 16 workers were killed.

On February 19th, a strain of the avian flu (H7) with low pathogenicity was first detected on a commercial chicken breeder farm in the Fraser Valley, BC. However, the strain experienced a significant shift in virulence and became highly pathogenic. This new strain was detected on the same farm on March 8th. By mid-May, 42 commercial farms and 11 backyard flocks were infected. In an effort to curb the rapid spread of the avian flu, more than 17 million birds (chickens, turkeys, ducks, geese and pigeons) were culled. Furthermore, two individuals were also infected. The outbreak lasted 91 days and had a gross economic cost of more than $380 million.

In late April of 1969, Trail, BC, experienced unseasonably high temperatures reaching 25C on April 22nd. Overnight and into the next day, over 24mm of rain also fell. With this, snowpacks on the Rossland Mountain Range quickly melted and inundated Trail Creek. At 3:45pm (local), after one of the culverts had been blocked, the floodwaters surged into the community. Within an hour, the entire downtown area was flooded. By 8:00pm, a second creek (Gorge Creek) also overtopped its banks. As a result, the downtown area was under 1.2-1.5m (4-5ft) of water. At 10:00pm, drastic measures were taken and four holes were blasted in the flood defences of the Columbia River in order to drain the water. In the early hours of April 24th, the flood was over. In total, 110 homes and 53 businesses were affected in addition to 77 damaged vehicles (26 beyond repair). Several buildings had their foundation undermined by the floodwaters including a three-storey (17 unit) apartment building which toppled over. Community streets and roadways were also damaged including roughly 2.5km that had been washed away or destabilized. The clean-up was substantial; in some locations, 1.5 m (5 ft) of mud, rock and sand was deposited on the streets. Furthermore, sewage from two other communities flowed into the flooded areas of Trail. While there were no deaths, 54 individuals including six infants and 10 seniors lost their homes. The flood is estimated to have caused $2.5 million (CAD 1969) in losses. The Premier of British Columbia asked the Government of Canada to declare the community a disaster area and requested federal contributions.

The winter and spring leading up to the flood season had higher than normal snowpacks across many regions of the Yukon. On June 9th, the Yukon Emergency Coordination Centre was activated as a result of the increasing flood risk. By July 13th, there were 16 flood events spanning across the entire Territory. On December 5th, the Yukon requested financial assistance from the federal government.

In mid-January, a cold wave affected the Yukon Territory. The most extreme period occurred at the end of January. Between January 27th and February 4th in Whitehorse, the mean temperature was below -40C. In Snag, the mean temperature was below -50C between January 29 and February 4 (with the exception of the 1st which was -49.7C). The lowest temperature ever recorded in North America was on the morning of February 3rd where the Snag Airport officially recorded -63C.
